encontrar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin incontrāre ('to meet face to face, come upon'), formed from the Latin phrase in contrā ('opposite, facing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encontrar

encontro.etymology: Deverbal noun from encontrar ('to meet, come across' < Late Latin incontrāre, from in contrā 'facing, opposite').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encontro

encostar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Romance from em- (< Latin in-) + costa ('rib, side, back, slope' < Latin costa 'rib, side') + -ar, meaning 'to lean one's side or back against, place alongside'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encostar

endereço.etymology: Deverbal noun from endereçar ('to direct straight, guide, address a letter' < Vulgar Latin *indīrēctiāre, from in- + dīrēctus 'straight, direct').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: endereço

enganar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingannāre ('to mock, trick, deceive'), related to Late Latin gannāre ('to jeer, mock') and Classical Latin gannīre ('to yelp, snarl').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enganar

engano.etymology: Deverbal noun from enganar ('to deceive, mislead; reflexively, to be mistaken' < Vulgar Latin *ingannāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: engano

engraçado.etymology: Participial adjective of engraçar ('to endow with charm or wit', from em- + graça 'grace, charm, humor' < Latin grātia), meaning 'funny, amusing, cute'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: engraçado

enorme.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēnormis ('out of rule, irregular, immense, vast'), compounded from ex- ('out of') + norma ('carpenter's square, rule, standard').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enorme

enquanto.etymology: Formed in Old Portuguese by fusing the phrase em quanto ('in how much [time], while, whereas' < Latin in quantō).

history.meaning: in how much, for as long as

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enquanto

enrolar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from em- (< Latin in-) + rolo ('roll, coil, cylinder' < Latin rotulus, diminutive of rota 'wheel') + -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enrolar

ensaiar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin exagiāre ('to weigh, test, try out'), derived from exagium ('a weighing, balance, trial' < Classical exigere), with replacement of initial ex- by en-.

history.meaning: weighing, trial / to test, try out

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ensaiar

ensolarado.etymology: Parasynthetic adjective formed in Portuguese from em- + solar ('of the sun', from sol < Latin sōl) + -ado, meaning 'bathed in sunshine, sunny'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ensolarado

entrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin intrāre ('to go inside, enter'), derived from the adverb/preposition intrā ('inside, within').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: entrar

entrega.etymology: Deverbal noun from entregar ('to hand over, deliver' < Latin integrāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: entrega

entregar.etymology: Inherited from Latin integrāre ('to make whole, restore intact', from integer 'whole, untouched'), with metathesis of -r-; shifted in Iberian Romance from 'restoring a pledge intact' to 'handing over, delivering'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: entregar

então.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intunce ('then, at that time'), an enlarged compound based on Classical Latin tunc ('then'), via Old Portuguese enton / entom.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: então

envelope.etymology: Borrowed from French enveloppe ('folded paper cover for a letter'), deverbal noun from envelopper ('to wrap up, enclose').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: envelope

equipe.etymology: Borrowed from French équipe ('work crew, team'), back-formed from équiper ('to outfit a ship or crew' < Old French esquiper, from Old Norse skipa 'to fit out a ship, man a vessel', from skip 'ship').

history.meaning: ship / to man a ship, outfit

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: equipe

erguido.etymology: Participial adjective of erguer ('to raise, lift up, set upright'), which descends from Vulgar Latin *ergere, syncopated from Classical Latin ērigere ('to raise up, erect').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: erguido

errado.etymology: Inherited from Latin errātus, past participle of errāre ('to wander, stray from the right path, make a mistake').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: errado

errar.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin errāre ('to wander aimlessly, go astray, miss the mark, make an error').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: errar

erro.etymology: Deverbal noun from errar ('to stray, make a mistake' < Latin errāre, alongside Classical Latin error).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: erro

erva.etymology: Inherited from Latin herba ('grass, green shoot, culinary or medicinal herb'), with regular spirantization of post-liquid -b- to -v-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: erva

escada.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scalāta ('flight of steps, ladder'), derived from Classical Latin scāla ('ladder, stairs', from scandere 'to climb'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escada

escala.etymology: Semi-learned descendant (or borrowing via Italian scala) of Latin scāla ('ladder, stair, graduated scale, port of call'), derived from scandere ('to climb').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escala

escola.etymology: Descends from Latin schola ('leisure devoted to learning, lecture, school'), borrowed from Ancient Greek skholḗ ('leisure, learned discussion, school').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escola

escolha.etymology: Deverbal noun from escolher ('to choose, select' < Vulgar Latin *excolligere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escolha

escolher.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excolligere ('to pick out from a group, select, choose'), compounded from ex- ('out of') + Classical Latin colligere ('to gather, collect').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escolher

esconder.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excondere, remodeled with prefix ex- from Classical Latin abscondere ('to put out of sight, hide away', from abs- + condere 'to store away').

history.meaning: to put out of sight, hide

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esconder

escondido.etymology: Participial adjective of esconder ('to hide, conceal' < Vulgar Latin *excondere < Classical Latin abscondere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escondido

escorregar.etymology: Shared with Galician and Spanish escorregar ('to slip, slide'); most often traced to a Vulgar Latin intensive verb *excurricāre (built on currere 'to run, slide') or a pre-Roman substrate formation.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escorregar

escrever.etymology: Inherited from Latin scrībere ('to trace, draw lines, write'), with prosthetic e- before the initial sC- cluster and spirantization of intervocalic -b- to -v-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escrever

escrito.etymology: Inherited from Latin scrīptus ('written'), past participle of scrībere ('to write').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escrito

escritório.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin scrīptōrium ('writing room, study, office'), derived from the supine stem of Latin scrībere ('to write').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escritório

esculpir.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin sculpere ('to carve, chisel, sculpt in stone or wood'), with prosthetic e- before initial sc-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esculpir

escuro.etymology: Inherited from Latin obscūrus ('dark, dim, shadowy'), via Vulgar Latin reduction of the initial cluster (*scūrus > escuro).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escuro

escutar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin ascultāre (dissimilated from Classical Latin auscultāre 'to listen attentively, lend an ear'), with prefix substitution to es-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escutar

esfriar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Portuguese from es- (< Latin ex-) + frio ('cold' < Latin frīgidus) + -ar, meaning 'to grow cold, cool down'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esfriar

espalhar.etymology: Formed in Romance from es- (< Latin ex-) + palha ('straw, chaff' < Latin palea) + -ar (compare Vulgar Latin *expandiculāre), originally meaning 'to scatter straw or chaff', hence 'to spread out, scatter'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espalhar

espaço.etymology: Espaço continues Latin spatium ('room, distance, interval of space or time'), with prosthetic e- before initial s + consonant.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espaço

espaço.notes: Ocupar espaço means 'to take up room'.

especial.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin speciālis ('individual, particular, special'), derived from speciēs ('appearance, kind, sort', from specere 'to look at').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: especial

espelho.etymology: Inherited from Latin speculum ('mirror, looking-glass'), an instrument noun derived from specere ('to look, behold'), with regular palatalization of -c'l- to -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espelho

esperar.etymology: Inherited from Latin spērāre ('to hope for, look forward to, expect'), which expanded semantically in Iberian Romance to include 'to wait for'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esperar

espiar.etymology: Borrowed via Romance from Frankish/Germanic *spehōn ('to look closely, watch, scout, spy on'), prefixed with es- (< Latin ex-).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espiar

esponja.etymology: From Latin spongia ('sponge'), borrowed from Greek spongiá, with regular prosthetic e- before initial sp-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esponja

esponja.notes: Used for natural sea sponges and household cleaning sponges alike.

esquecer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excadescere ('to fall out of the mind, slip from memory'), formed from ex- ('out of') + cadere ('to fall') + inchoative suffix -ēscere.

history.meaning: to drop out of memory, forget

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquecer

esquentar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excalentāre ('to make warm, heat up'), built on calēns, calentis, the present participle of Classical Latin calēre ('to be warm, hot').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquentar

esquerda.etymology: Substantivized feminine of esquerdo ('left'), elliptically from mão esquerda ('left hand, left-hand side').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquerda

esquerdo.etymology: Shared across Iberian Romance (Spanish izquierdo, Catalan esquerre); borrowed from a pre-Roman Vasconic/Pyrenean substrate closely related to Basque ezker ('left').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquerdo

esquina.etymology: Borrowed via Western Romance from Germanic *skina ('shinbone, narrow strip, sharp ridge or angle'), naming the outward-projecting angle where two walls or streets meet.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquina

esse.etymology: Inherited from Latin ipse ('he himself, that very one'), which shifted in Iberian Romance to become the second-person/medial demonstrative ('that [near you or just mentioned]').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esse

estalo.etymology: Deverbal noun from estalar ('to crack, snap, pop, burst'), an expressive formation imitating a sharp snapping sound (also compared with Old French estaler).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estalo

estante.etymology: Originally the present participle of estar (< Latin stāns, stantis 'standing upright', from stāre 'to stand'), substantivized to name a standing book-rest, lectern, or shelving unit.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estante

estar.etymology: Priberam traces estar to Latin sto, stare, with meanings concerning standing, remaining or staying firm. Modern estar also expresses location and presence, including being at a meeting. Its history does not limit it to standing upright.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estar

estação.etymology: Learned or semi-learned descendant of Latin statiō, statiōnis ('a standing still, post, stopping place, season'), derived from stāre ('to stand').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estação

este.etymology: Inherited from Latin iste ('that of yours'), which shifted in Vulgar Latin to become the first-person proximal demonstrative ('this [near me]').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: este

estouro.etymology: Deverbal noun from estourar ('to burst, explode, roar'), commonly traced by philologists to a Vulgar Latin *extaurāre ('to bellow or charge like a bull', from taurus 'bull') or an expressive root.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estouro

estrada.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin (via) strāta ('paved road built of layered stone'), the feminine past participle of Classical Latin sternere ('to spread out, strew, pave').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estrada

estragar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin strāgāre ('to lay waste, ruin, spoil'), derived from Classical Latin strāgēs ('overthrow, devastation, wreckage', related to sternere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estragar

estranho.etymology: Inherited from Latin extrāneus ('external, foreign, strange, unfamiliar'), derived from extrā ('outside, beyond').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estranho

estreia.etymology: Deverbal noun from estrear ('to use or perform for the first time, inaugurate'), derived from Old Portuguese estrea ('auspicious gift, New Year's present' < Latin strēna 'good omen, New Year's gift').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estreia

estreito.etymology: Inherited from Latin strictus ('drawn tight, close, narrow'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight, bind, squeeze').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estreito

estrela.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stēlla / *strella (Classical Latin stēlla, 'star', with intrusive -r- likely influenced by astro).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estrela

estúdio.etymology: Borrowed from Italian studio and English studio ('artist's workroom, recording or broadcast room'), a specialized descendant of Latin studium ('zeal, study, room for study').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estúdio

etiqueta.etymology: Borrowed from French étiquette ('attached label, price tag, court ceremonial'), from Old French estiquette ('small note stuck to a file', from estiquer 'to stick, pin' < Middle Dutch steken 'to prick, stick').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: etiqueta

eu.etymology: The subject pronoun continues Latin ego. Priberam treats it separately from same-spelled learned word-building elements. The speaker uses the ordinary personal pronoun when identifying his own department.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: eu

exatamente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the feminine adjective exata ('exact, accurate' < Latin exāctus) + adverbial suffix -mente.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: exatamente

exato.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin exāctus ('measured out, precise, accurate'), past participle of exigere ('to drive out, weigh, measure accurately').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: exato

experimentar.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin expērīmentāre ('to test, put to the proof, try out'), derived from Classical Latin expērīmentum ('trial, proof, test').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: experimentar

experiência.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin experientia ('trial, proof, knowledge gained by practice'), derived from experīrī ('to try, test thoroughly').

history.meaning: to try, put to the test

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: experiência

explicar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin explicāre ('to unfold, unroll a scroll, set forth clearly, explain'), compounded from ex- ('out') + plicāre ('to fold').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: explicar

expresso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin expressus ('pressed out, clearly stated; in modern usage via French/English, fast direct train or pressed coffee'), past participle of exprimere ('to press out, express').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: expresso

extra.etymology: From Latin extrā ('outside, beyond, in addition to'), reinforced in modern usage as an adjective and noun by international shortening of extraordinário.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: extra

fachada.etymology: Borrowed from Italian facciata ('front wall of a building, facade'), derived from faccia ('face' < Vulgar Latin *facia, Classical faciēs).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fachada

falante.etymology: Present participial adjective and noun of falar ('to speak, talk' < Late Latin fābulāre), denoting 'talkative, speaking' or a 'speaker (of a language or loudspeaker)'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: falante

falar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin fābulāre (Classical deponent fābulārī 'to converse, chat, tell stories'), from fābula ('talk, story', from fārī 'to speak'), via syncope and loss of -b'- (fābulāre > fablar > falar).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: falar

falta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fallita ('shortcoming, failure, lack'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin fallere ('to deceive, fail, be lacking').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: falta

faltar.etymology: Derived from the noun falta ('lack, absence, shortcoming' < Vulgar Latin *fallita, from Latin fallere 'to fail, be wanting') + verbal suffix -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: faltar

familiar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin familiāris ('belonging to a household, domestic, intimate, well-known'), derived from familia ('household, family').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: familiar

família.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin familia ('household establishment, kin and servants under one roof'), derived from famulus ('household servant, attendant').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: família

farmácia.etymology: Learned borrowing via Medieval Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeía ('preparation or use of medicines'), derived from phármakon ('medicinal herb, drug, remedy').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: farmácia

fatia.etymology: Origin uncertain in Priberam; widely connected by Iberian etymologists with Arabic fatīlah / fatīta ('crumb, piece of broken bread') or a Vulgar Latin derivative.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fatia

favor.etymology: Borrowed from Latin favor, favōris ('goodwill, partiality, support, kindness'), derived from the verb favēre ('to be favorable to, support').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: favor

favorito.etymology: Borrowed from Italian favorito ('favored one, favorite'), past participle of favorire ('to favor', from favore < Latin favor).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: favorito

fazer.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin facere ('to make, do, perform').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fazer

fechado.etymology: Participial adjective of fechar ('to close, shut, lock' < Vulgar Latin *pessulāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fechado

fechadura.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from fechar ('to lock, close' < Vulgar Latin *pessulāre) + instrument suffix -dura, naming a door lock.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fechadura

fechar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pessulāre ('to bolt a door'), derived from Classical Latin pessulus ('door bolt' < Ancient Greek pássalos 'peg, bolt'), with alteration of initial p- to f- (influenced by ferro or firmāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fechar

feio.etymology: Inherited from Latin foedus ('foul, unseemly, ugly, deformed'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -d- (foedu > feo > feio).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feio

feira.etymology: Priberam derives feira from Late Latin feria ('holiday, feast day'), because medieval markets gathered around church feast days—the same liturgical root that gave Portuguese its weekday names (segunda-feira to sexta-feira).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feira

feira.notes: In Brazil, a feira (or feira livre) is the neighbourhood open-air street market.

feito.etymology: Inherited from Latin factus ('made, done'), past participle of facere ('to make, do'), with regular vocalization of preconsonantal -c- (factu > feito).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feito

feliz.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin fēlīx, fēlīcis ('fruitful, auspicious, fortunate, happy').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feliz

feltro.etymology: Via Medieval Latin filtrum from West Germanic *filtir ('pressed, unspun wool').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feltro

feltro.notes: In pianos, dense wool felt cushions each wooden hammer so strings ring warmly instead of clinking.

fenda.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *findita ('cleft, crack, split') or formed as a deverbal noun from fender ('to split, cleave' < Classical Latin findere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fenda

ferragem.etymology: Derived from ferro ('iron' < Latin ferrum) + collective suffix -agem (< Latin -āticum via Gallo-Romance), denoting ironwork or metal hardware fittings.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ferragem

ferramenta.etymology: Inherited from Latin ferrāmenta ('iron implements, tools'), originally the neuter plural of ferrāmentum ('iron tool', from ferrum 'iron'), reanalyzed in Romance as a feminine singular noun.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ferramenta

ferro.etymology: Direct continuation of Latin ferrum ('iron'), preserving Latin initial f- intact.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ferro

ferro.notes: Compare Spanish hierro, where Castilian lost initial f- and diphthongized short ĕ.

ficar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *figicāre ('to drive in, fix firmly in place'), derived from Classical Latin fīgere ('to fasten, fix'); shifted semantically from 'being fixed in place' to 'staying, remaining, becoming'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ficar

fila.etymology: Borrowed from French file ('row, line of persons or things one behind another'), deverbal from filer ('to spin thread in a line' < Late Latin fīlāre, from fīlum 'thread').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fila

fim.etymology: Inherited from Latin fīnis, fīnem ('boundary, border, limit, end').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fim

formal.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin fōrmālis ('pertaining to form, following established rules, official'), derived from fōrma ('shape, mold, pattern, rule').

foto.etymology: Colloquial clipping of fotografia ('photograph'), compounded from Ancient Greek phôs, phōtós ('light') + -graphía ('drawing, writing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: garoar

gastar.etymology: Inherited from Latin vāstāre ('to lay waste, ravage, use up, spend'), crossed phonetically in Vulgar Latin with Germanic *wōstijan (yielding initial g-).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: gastar

gaveta.etymology: Diminutive derivative of Late Latin gabata ('wooden bowl, trough, shallow tray'), which shifted semantically in Portuguese to a sliding cabinet drawer.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: infelizmente

infância.etymology: From Latin infantia (childhood, literally 'inability to speak').

inglês.etymology: Borrowed via Old French angleis / engleis from Medieval Latin Anglicus (matching Old English Englisc, 'of the Angles, English').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: inglês

inicial.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin initiālis ('pertaining to the beginning, initial'), derived from Classical Latin initium ('beginning, entrance', from inīre 'to enter upon').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: inicial

inspetor.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin inspector, inspectōris ('observer, overseer, examiner'), agent noun of inspicere ('to look into, examine').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: inspetor

instante.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin īnstāns, īnstantis ('standing near, pressing, present moment'), present participle of īnstāre ('to stand upon, be close at hand').

history.meaning: to be close at hand, press upon

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: instante

inteiro.etymology: Inherited from Latin integer, integrum ('untouched, whole, complete, intact'), with vocalization of preconsonantal -g- (integru > enteiro > inteiro).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: inteiro

interno.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin internus ('inward, internal, domestic'), derived from inter ('between, within').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: interno

interruptor.etymology: Adapted from French interrupteur ('circuit breaker, electrical switch'), built on Latin interruptus, past participle of interrumpere ('to break off, interrupt', from inter- + rumpere 'to break').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: interruptor

inverno.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin hībernum (tempus) ('wintry season, winter'), from Classical Latin hībernus ('of winter'), with nasal epenthesis in the initial syllable (iverno > inverno).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: inverno

ir.etymology: The infinitive belongs to the Latin eo, ire family for going. Modern Portuguese ir has very different-looking inflected forms, so its conjugation is not a sequence of regular changes to the written infinitive. The scene uses vou and vai.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ir

irmão.etymology: Inherited from Latin germānus ('full brother born of the same parents'), which replaced Classical frāter for literal kinship in Iberian Romance (compare Spanish hermano).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: irmão

irmãozinho.etymology: Diminutive of irmão ('brother' < Latin germānus) formed with the Portuguese diminutive suffix -zinho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: irmãozinho

isolante.etymology: Derived from isolar ('to isolate, insulate' < Italian isolare, from isola 'island' < Latin īnsula) + present participial suffix -nte, naming an electrical or thermal insulator.

history.meaning: to set apart like an island

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: isolante

isso.etymology: Inherited from Latin ipsum, neuter singular of ipse ('that very thing, itself'), serving as the Portuguese neuter medial demonstrative pronoun ('that').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: isso

isto.etymology: Inherited from Latin istud, neuter singular of iste ('this thing [near the speaker]').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: isto

jamais.etymology: Formed from or modeled on Old French/Occitan jamais ('ever, never'), compounding já ('already, ever' < Latin iam) + mais ('more' < Latin magis).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jamais

janela.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *januĕlla ('small opening, little doorway'), diminutive of Classical Latin jānua ('door, arched passage', linked to Janus, Roman god of thresholds and beginnings).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: janela

janela.notes: Distinctive to Portuguese and Galician (compare Spanish ventana < ventus 'wind', French fenêtre < fenestra).

jantar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *iantāre, reduced from Classical Latin ientāre ('to eat an early morning meal, breakfast'); over time the meal shifted from morning to midday and finally to evening dinner.

history.meaning: to eat the morning meal -> to dine

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jantar

jardim.etymology: Priberam derives jardim from French jardin. The French word has a Germanic root meaning an enclosed plot, the same family as English garden and yard. Brazilian jardim de inverno, literally winter garden, names a glassed-in sunroom.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jardim

jarra.etymology: Borrowed via Andalusi Arabic ǧárra from Classical Arabic jarrah ('earthenware water jar, pitcher').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jarra

jeito.etymology: Inherited from Latin iactus ('a throwing, cast, gesture, movement'), derived from iacere ('to throw'), with regular vocalization of -c- (iactu > jeito), evolving from 'throw, bearing' to 'manner, knack, way'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jeito

jogado.etymology: Participial adjective of jogar ('to play, throw, toss' < Vulgar Latin iocāre, Classical deponent iocārī).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jogado

jogar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin iocāre (Classical deponent iocārī 'to jest, joke, play', from iocus 'jest, game'), which replaced Classical lūdere for 'to play' and in Portuguese also came to mean 'to throw, toss'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jogar

jornal.etymology: Priberam records jornal as a borrowing from French journal ('daily paper'), ultimately from Late Latin diurnalis ('daily', from dies, 'day').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jornal

jornal.notes: In Brazil o jornal means both a printed newspaper and a televised news broadcast.

jovem.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin iuvenis, iuvenem ('young, youthful; young person').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jovem

junta.etymology: Substantivized feminine of junto (< Latin iūncta, feminine past participle of iungere 'to join, yoke'), naming a joint, seam, sealing gasket, or board.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: junta

juntar.etymology: Formed in Romance from junto ('joined, together' < Latin iūnctus) + verbal suffix -ar (< Vulgar Latin *iūnctāre 'to join together, gather').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: juntar

junto.etymology: Inherited from Latin iūnctus ('joined, yoked together, united'), past participle of iungere ('to join, yoke').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: junto

justo.etymology: Learned or semi-learned descendant of Latin iūstus ('righteous, fair, exact, snug'), derived from iūs ('law, right').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: justo

já.etymology: Inherited from Latin iam ('already, now, right away'), with regular palatalization of initial i- before a vowel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: já

lado.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *latum (remodeling of Classical Latin neuter latus, lateris 'side, flank'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lado

lance.etymology: Deverbal noun from lançar ('to throw, cast, launch; to bid at an auction' < Late Latin lanceāre 'to hurl a lance', from lancea 'spear'), naming a throw, flight of stairs, play, or bid.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lance

lanterna.etymology: From Latin lanterna ('lantern, lamp'), borrowed from Ancient Greek lamptḗr ('torch, beacon', from lámpō 'to shine') via Etruscan mediation.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lanterna

laranja.etymology: From Andalusi Arabic naranǧa (Classical Arabic nāranjah 'bitter orange', from Persian nārang < Sanskrit nāraṅga), with dissimilation of initial n- to l- in Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: laranja

largo.etymology: Inherited from Latin largus ('abundant, bountiful, wide, spacious').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: largo

largura.etymology: Derived in Romance from largo ('wide, broad' < Latin largus) + abstract suffix -ura, meaning 'width, breadth'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: largura

lata.etymology: Originally 'thin wooden lath or metal strip' (borrowed via Romance from Germanic *latta 'lath, strip'), later used elliptically for folha de lata ('tin-plated iron sheet') and 'tin can'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lata

latão.etymology: Borrowed via Old French laton or Spanish latón ('brass'), traced to Arabic lāṭūn ('copper, brass', itself from Turkic altun 'gold, gleaming yellow metal').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: latão

lavar.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin lavāre ('to wash, bathe, cleanse').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lavar

legume.etymology: Descends from Latin legūmen, legūminis ('podded plant, pulse, bean, vegetable', connected with legere 'to gather, pick by hand').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: legume

lei.etymology: Inherited from Latin lēx, lēgem ('law, statute, rule'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -g- (lēge > lee > lei).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lei

leite.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lacte (for Classical Latin lac, lactis 'milk'), with regular vocalization of preconsonantal -c- (lacte > leite).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: leite

leitura.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned from Medieval Latin lectūra ('a reading, commentary, text'), derived from Classical Latin legere, lēctum ('to read').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: leitura

lembrança.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from lembrar ('to remember, remind' < Latin memorāre) + abstract suffix -ança (< Latin -antia), denoting a memory, regards, or souvenir.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lembrança

lembrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin memorāre ('to bring to mind, recount, remember', from memor 'mindful'), via syncope, epenthesis of -b-, and dissimilation of initial m- to l- (memorāre > membrar > nembrar > lembrar).

history.meaning: mindful / to bring to mind, remember

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lembrar

lente.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lēns, lentis ('lentil'), applied in optics since the 17th century because curved glass lenses share the biconvex shape of a lentil seed.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lente

lente.notes: Etymological twin of the inherited culinary word lentilha (< lenticŭla).

lentilha.etymology: From Latin lenticŭla ('little lentil'), diminutive of lens, lentis ('lentil'), with regular palatalization of -c'l- to -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lentilha

lentilha.notes: Optical lenses (lentes) were named after the curved shape of a lentil.

lento.etymology: Inherited from Latin lentus ('pliable, tough, slow-moving, unhurried').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lento

lençol.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin linteolum ('small linen cloth, bedsheet'), diminutive of Classical Latin linteum ('linen cloth', derived from līnum 'flax, linen').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lençol

ler.etymology: Inherited from Latin legere ('to gather, pick out with the eyes, read'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -g- and contraction (legere > leer > ler).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ler

letra.etymology: Inherited from Latin littera ('written character, letter of the alphabet; in plural, epistle, learning').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: letra

letrinha.etymology: Diminutive of letra ('letter, written character' < Latin littera) formed with the suffix -inha, often used for small or fine print.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: letrinha

levantar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *levantāre ('to raise, lift up'), built on levāns, levantis, present participle of Classical Latin levāre ('to lighten, lift', from levis 'light').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: levantar

levar.etymology: Inherited from Latin levāre ('to lighten, lift up, raise, carry away', from levis 'light in weight'), which became the general Portuguese verb for 'to carry, take'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: levar

leve.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin levis, leve ('light in weight, slight, gentle').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: leve

licença.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin licentia ('freedom, permission, leave'), derived from licēre ('to be lawful, be permitted').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: licença

ligado.etymology: Participial adjective of ligar ('to bind, connect, switch on, pay heed' < Latin ligāre).

history.meaning: to bind / bound, connected, switched on

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ligado

ligar.etymology: From Latin ligāre ('to bind, tie fast, unite'), extended in modern Portuguese to 'to connect, switch on an electrical device, call by telephone, pay attention to'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ligar

limpar.etymology: Derived from limpo ('clean' < Latin limpidus) + verbal suffix -ar (or from Late Latin limpidāre 'to make clear, cleanse').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: limpar

limpinho.etymology: Diminutive of limpo ('clean, neat' < Latin limpidus) formed with the suffix -inho, meaning 'spotless, nice and clean'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: limpinho

limpo.etymology: Inherited from Latin limpidus ('clear, transparent, pure, clean'), via early syncope of the post-tonic vowel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: limpo

limão.etymology: Entered Iberian Romance through Andalusi Arabic laymūn, from Persian līmūn ('citrus fruit, lemon/lime').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: limão

lindo.etymology: From Old Portuguese lindo ('legitimate, pure, genuine, fine, beautiful'), inherited from Latin lēgitimus ('lawful, genuine, proper') via syncopated Hispano-Romance *lēg'dimu > lindo.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lindo

linha.etymology: Inherited from Latin līnea ('linen thread, string, plumb-line, drawn line'), feminine of līneus ('made of flax', from līnum 'flax, linen').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: linha

lista.etymology: Borrowed via Western Romance (*lista 'strip, border, catalog strip') from Proto-Germanic *līstō ('hem, strip, border').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lista

livre.etymology: Descends from Latin līber, līberum ('free, unconstrained, independent'), reinforced by Gallo-Romance libre.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: livre

livro.etymology: Inherited from Latin liber, librum ('inner bark of a tree used for writing, scroll, book').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: livro

lixa.etymology: Originally named the shagreen or rough placoid-scaled skin of the dogfish shark (lixa, a word of uncertain pre-Roman origin) used by cabinetmakers to abrade wood, later transferred to 'sandpaper' and 'nail file'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lixa

lixar.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from lixa ('sandpaper, originally rough sharkskin') + verbal suffix -ar, meaning 'to sand, smooth with sandpaper'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lixar

lixo.etymology: From Old Portuguese lixo ('dirty lye-water, ashes, sediment, filth'), derived from Latin līx, līcis ('ashes, lye') or līxivium ('ash-lye used for scrubbing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lixo

locomotiva.etymology: Borrowed from French locomotive / English locomotive (engine), formed from Modern Latin locōmōtīvus (from Latin ablative locō 'from a place' + mōtus 'moved', from movēre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: locomotiva

logo.etymology: The time adverb is traced to Latin locus, meaning place. Priberam treats it separately from the modern shortening of logótipo and other same-spelled learned elements. In até logo it refers to seeing someone again soon or later, not to a visual brand mark.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: logo

loja.etymology: Borrowed from Old French loge ('arbor, covered gallery, ground-floor merchant's booth or shop'), from Frankish *laubja ('shelter of boughs, porch, stall').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: loja

longe.etymology: Inherited from Latin longē ('far off, at a distance'), adverb of longus ('long').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: longe

lotado.etymology: Participial adjective of lotar ('to divide into shares, fix or fill the capacity of a vehicle or venue'), derived from lote ('share, allotment' < French lot < Frankish *hlot 'lot, portion').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lotado

lugar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin locālis ('belonging to a place, spot', from Classical Latin locus 'place'), with dissimilation of final -l to -r (logal > logar > lugar).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lugar

luminária.etymology: From Late Latin lūmināria ('lamps, lights'), neuter plural of Classical Latin lūmināre ('lamp, light-giving body', from lūmen 'light') reinterpreted as a feminine singular noun.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: luminária

lustrar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin lūstrāre ('to purify, illuminate, make bright', reinforced by Italian lustrare 'to polish, shine').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lustrar

luz.etymology: Inherited from Latin lūx, lūcis ('light, daylight, brightness').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: luz

lá.etymology: Inherited from Latin illāc ('that way, over there', ablative feminine of ille + locative -c), with apheresis of the unstressed initial syllable (elá > lá).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lá

lápis.etymology: Borrowed from Italian lapis ('hematite chalk, drawing crayon, pencil', short for lapis ematite), from Latin lapis, lapidis ('stone').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lápis

lâmpada.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Late Latin lampada (Classical accusative of lampas, lampadis 'torch, oil lamp'), borrowed from Ancient Greek lampás, lampádos ('torch, lamp', from lámpō 'to shine').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lâmpada

lã.etymology: From Latin lāna ('wool'), showing classic Galician-Portuguese nasalization of the stressed vowel before intervocalic -n- followed by loss of -n- (lāna > lãa > lã).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lã

lã.notes: Compare irmão (< germānum) and mão (< mănum) for the same sound change.

machucar.etymology: Formed in Iberian Romance as an expressive derivative of macho ('heavy pounding hammer' < Latin marculus 'small hammer'), meaning 'to pound, crush, bruise, hurt'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: machucar

macio.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from Vulgar Latin *mattīcius ('softened, tenderized', from Late Latin mattus 'sodden, limp, softened') or related to maço ('mallet used to beat flax soft').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: macio

madeira.etymology: Inherited from Latin matĕria ('building timber, tree trunk wood, substance'), via voicing -t- > -d- and yod metathesis -ri- > -ir-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: madeira

madeira.notes: Inspired the name of the wooded Atlantic island of Madeira and pairs with learned doublet matéria.

maio.etymology: Inherited from Latin (mēnsis) Māius ('month of May', traditionally named after the Italic earth goddess Maia).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: maio

maior.etymology: Inherited from Latin māior, māiōrem ('greater, larger, elder'), the irregular comparative of magnus ('large, great').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: maior

mais.etymology: Inherited from Latin magis ('more, to a greater degree'), with regular palatalization and loss of intervocalic -g- (magis > mais).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mais

mal.etymology: Inherited from Latin male ('badly, ill, wrongly', adverb of malus 'bad') and malum ('evil, harm, ailment'), with regular apocope of final -e.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mal

mala.etymology: Borrowed from Old French male (modern malle, 'leather travelling bag, trunk'), from Frankish *malha ('leather pouch, wallet, travelling sack').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mala

mancha.etymology: Inherited from Latin macula ('spot, stain, blemish'), via syncopated *mac'la with palatalization of -cl- to -ch- and nasal epenthesis from the initial m-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mancha

mandar.etymology: Inherited from Latin mandāre ('to put into someone's hand, entrust, command, send', from manus 'hand' + dare 'to give, put').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mandar

manga.etymology: Converges two unrelated etyma: (1) 'sleeve', inherited from Latin manica ('long sleeve covering the hand', from manus 'hand'); (2) 'mango fruit', borrowed during 16th-century trade in Malabar from Malayalam māṅṅa / Tamil māṅkāy.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: manga

manhã.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(hōra) māneāna ('early morning hour'), derived from the Classical Latin adverb/indeclinable noun māne ('early in the morning').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: manhã

manteiga.etymology: Shared with Asturian-Leonese manteiga and Spanish manteca ('butter, fat'), inherited from a pre-Roman Paleohispanic substrate word *mantaica ('butter').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: manteiga

manter.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin manūtenēre (from the Classical phrase manū tenēre 'to hold in the hand, support, preserve', from ablative manū 'by hand' + tenēre 'to hold').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: manter

manutenção.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin manūtentiō, manūtentiōnis ('a holding in the hand, support, upkeep, maintenance'), the action noun corresponding to manter.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: manutenção

maravilha.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin mīrābilia ('wonderful things, marvels'), the neuter plural of Classical Latin mīrābilis ('wonderful, astonishing', from mīrārī 'to wonder at') reanalyzed as a feminine singular noun.

history.meaning: to wonder at / wonderful things, marvels

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: maravilha

maravilhoso.etymology: Derived from maravilha ('marvel, wonder' < Latin mīrābilia) + adjectival suffix -oso (< Latin -ōsus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: maravilhoso

marca.etymology: Borrowed via Western Romance from Germanic *marka ('boundary sign, mark, brand, token').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marca

marcar.etymology: Borrowed via Western Romance (*markāre) from Germanic *markōn ('to set a boundary sign, stamp a mark, schedule').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marcar

marceneiro.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from marcenaria ('fine woodworking, cabinetmaking'), historically linked to Medieval Latin mercēnārius / Romance merceria ('skilled craftwork, trade') specialized for fine joinery.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marceneiro

marfim.etymology: From Old Portuguese marfil / marfim, borrowed from Andalusi Arabic (ʿaẓm) al-fīl ('bone/tusk of the elephant'), where al-fīl ('the elephant') comes from Persian pīl.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marfim

marinho.etymology: Inherited from Latin marīnus ('of the sea, marine'), derived from mare ('sea'), with palatalization of intervocalic -n- in Galician-Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marinho

marketing.etymology: An English loanword, explicitly identified as English by Priberam. Portuguese uses it for the business activity and field. No claim about an earlier borrowing date or an unverified ancient root is needed to explain this recorded source.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marketing

marrom.etymology: Borrowed in Brazilian Portuguese from French marron ('chestnut-colored, brown', literally 'large sweet chestnut' < Italian marrone).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marrom

martelinho.etymology: Diminutive of martelo ('hammer' < Late Latin martellus, diminutive of marculus 'small hammer') formed with the suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: martelinho

martelo.etymology: From Late Latin martĕllus ('hammer'), diminutive of martŭlus / marcus ('hammer').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: martelo

martelo.notes: Names both a carpenter's hammer and the felt-covered wooden hammer inside a piano action.

mas.etymology: The contrasting conjunction comes from Latin magis, meaning more. Its modern use introduces a different or qualifying point. Priberam gives another entry for a same-spelled pronoun contraction; that is not the conjunction in mas valeu.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mas

massa.etymology: Inherited from Latin massa ('kneaded lump, dough, paste, mass'), borrowed from Ancient Greek mâza ('barley cake, lump of kneaded dough', from mássō 'to knead').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: massa

maçaneta.etymology: Diminutive derivative of maçã ('apple' < Vulgar Latin *mattiāna; compare Italian mazzanetta), naming a round, apple-shaped doorknob or pommel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: maçaneta

maçã.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(māla) mattiāna ('Mattian apple', a sweet apple cultivar named after the 1st-century BC Roman author Gaius Matius), via Old Portuguese maçãa.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: maçã

me.etymology: Inherited from Latin mē ('me'), the accusative/ablative singular of the first-person pronoun ego.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: me

medir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *metīre, an active remodeling of the Classical Latin deponent verb mētīrī ('to measure, measure out').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: medir

medo.etymology: Inherited from Latin metus, metum ('fear, dread, anxiety'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: medo

medroso.etymology: Derived in Iberian Romance from medo ('fear' < Latin metus, with epenthetic -r- modeled on pavoroso / temeroso) + adjectival suffix -oso (< Latin -ōsus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: medroso

meia-noite.etymology: Compound noun continuing Late Latin media nox, mediam noctem ('middle of the night, midnight', from medius 'middle, half' + nox, noctis 'night').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: meia-noite

meia-volta.etymology: Compound noun formed in Portuguese from meia ('half', feminine of meio < Latin medius) + volta ('turn' < Vulgar Latin *volta, from volvere 'to turn'), meaning 'half-turn, about-face'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: meia-volta

meio.etymology: Inherited from Latin medius ('middle, half, intermediate'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -d- (mediu > meo > meio).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: meio

meio-dia.etymology: Compound noun formed from meio ('middle, half' < Latin medius) + dia ('day' < Vulgar Latin *dia, Classical diēs), continuing Latin medius diēs ('midday, noon').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: meio-dia

mel.etymology: Mel descends directly from Latin mel, mellis ('honey').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mel

mel.notes: Masculine noun in Portuguese (o mel escuro), unlike feminine Spanish la miel.

melhor.etymology: Inherited from Latin melior, meliōrem ('better'), the irregular comparative of bonus ('good'), with regular palatalization of -li- to -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: melhor

melodia.etymology: Priberam traces melodia through Late Latin melodia to Greek melōidía ('singing, musical tune').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: melodia

melodia.notes: Stressed on -di- without needing a written accent under Portuguese spelling rules.

menino.etymology: From Old Portuguese meninho / menino ('child, infant, young page'), an expressive Iberian formation built on a nursery/diminutive stem *minn- ('small, little').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: menino

menor.etymology: Descends from Latin minor, minōrem ('smaller, lesser, younger'), the irregular comparative of parvus ('small').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: menor

menos.etymology: Inherited from Latin minus ('less'), the neuter comparative corresponding to minor ('smaller').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: menos

mercadinho.etymology: Diminutive of mercado ('market, grocery store' < Latin mercātus 'trade, marketplace', from mercārī 'to trade', from merx 'merchandise') formed with the suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mercadinho

merecer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *merēscere, an inchoative extension of Classical Latin merēre / merērī ('to earn, deserve, merit').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: merecer

mesa.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin mēsa, reduced from Classical Latin mēnsa ('table, dining board').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mesa

mesinha.etymology: Diminutive of mesa ('table' < Latin mēnsa) formed with the Portuguese diminutive suffix -inha.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mesinha

mesmo.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus ('he himself, the very same'), a superlative reinforcement of the intensive pronoun combination *met-ipse (extracted from egomet ipse).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mesmo

metade.etymology: Inherited from Latin medietās, medietātem ('the middle, half', derived from medius 'middle, half'), via Old Portuguese meiadade > metade.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: metade

metal.etymology: Descends from Latin metallum ('mine, quarry, mineral, metal'), borrowed from Ancient Greek métallon ('mine, quarry, metal').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: metal

metro.etymology: Borrowed from French mètre ('meter, base unit of length'), coined in the 1790s from Ancient Greek métron ('measure, standard').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: metro

metálico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin metallicus, from Ancient Greek metallikós ('pertaining to mines or metal'), derived from métallon ('mine, metal').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: metálico

meu.etymology: Inherited from Latin meus, meum ('my, mine').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: meu

mexer.etymology: Inherited from Latin miscēre ('to mix, mingle, stir up, disturb'), with palatalization of -sc- before a front vowel to -x- [ʃ].

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mexer

mexido.etymology: Participial adjective and noun of mexer ('to stir, mix, scramble, move' < Latin miscēre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mexido

milímetro.etymology: Borrowed from French millimètre, coined in the metric system from Latin mīlle ('thousand', combining form milli- 'one thousandth') + Ancient Greek métron ('measure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: milímetro

mim.etymology: Inherited from Latin mihi (contracted in Vulgar Latin to mī, 'to me'), dative singular of ego, with final nasalization assimilated from the initial m-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mim

minuto.etymology: From Medieval Latin (pars) minūta (prīma) ('first small division [of an hour or degree]'), feminine past participle of Classical Latin minuere ('to lessen, make small').

history.meaning: to make small / small division, minute

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: minuto

misterioso.etymology: Derived from mistério ('mystery' < Latin mystērium < Ancient Greek mystḗrion 'secret rite, secret') + adjectival suffix -oso (< Latin -ōsus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: misterioso

moderno.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin modernus ('of the present time, modern'), derived from the Classical Latin adverb modo ('just now, recently', originally ablative of modus 'measure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: moderno

moeda.etymology: Moeda develops from Latin moneta ('mint, coin') through regular loss of intervocalic -n- between vowels in Galician-Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: moeda

moeda.notes: Means both an individual metal coin and a country's currency.

molhado.etymology: Participial adjective of molhar ('to wet, soak, dampen' < Vulgar Latin *molliāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: molhado

molhar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *molliāre ('to soften by steeping in liquid, wet, soak'), derived from Classical Latin mollis ('soft, pliant').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: molhar

montanha.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *montānea ('mountainous region, mountain'), substantivized feminine of *montāneus ('of a mountain'), derived from Classical Latin mōns, montis ('mountain').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: montanha

morango.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from mora / amora ('mulberry, brambleberry' < Late Latin mōra, from Classical mōrum) + suffix -ango, naming the fragrant red strawberry.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: morango

morar.etymology: Inherited from Latin morārī ('to linger, stay, tarry, dwell, reside'), derived from mora ('delay, stay').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: morar

mordida.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of morder ('to bite' < Latin mordēre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mordida

morno.etymology: Origin uncertain in Priberam; specific to Galician-Portuguese ('lukewarm, tepid'), variously traced to a pre-Roman or Germanic stem *murn- ('gentle, dull') or a Vulgar Latin derivative.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: morno

morrer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *morīre (adapted to the -er conjugation in Iberian Romance as morrer), active remodeling of Classical Latin deponent morī ('to die').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: morrer

morro.etymology: Shared with Spanish morro ('snout, rounded knoll, headland'), traced to a pre-Roman substrate word *murro ('projecting snout, rounded hill').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: morro

mostrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin mōnstrāre ('to point out, show, indicate'), derived from mōnstrum ('divine sign, omen', from monēre 'to warn, advise').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mostrar

motivo.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin mōtīvus ('moving, impelling; as a noun, moving cause, reason'), derived from Classical Latin movēre, mōtum ('to move').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: motivo

motor.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin mōtor, mōtōris ('mover, one that imparts motion'), agent noun of Classical Latin movēre, mōtum ('to move').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: motor

motorista.etymology: Formed from motor ('engine, motor' < Late Latin mōtor) + occupational suffix -ista, naming a motor-vehicle driver.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: motorista

mudança.etymology: Derived in Romance from mudar ('to change, move' < Latin mūtāre) + abstract suffix -ança (< Latin -antia), denoting a change or household move.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mudança

mudar.etymology: Inherited from Latin mūtāre ('to change, alter, exchange, move from one place to another'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mudar

mudo.etymology: Inherited from Latin mūtus ('silent, speechless, mute'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mudo

muito.etymology: Inherited from Latin multus, multum ('much, many, very'), with regular vocalization of preconsonantal -l- (multu > muito) and progressive nasalization from initial m-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: muito

mulher.etymology: Inherited from Latin mulĭer, muliĕris (accusative muliĕrem, 'woman, wife'), with Vulgar Latin stress shift onto -ĕ- and palatalization -li- > -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mulher

mulher.notes: Preserves open stressed [ɛ] in Brazilian and European Portuguese alike.

mundo.etymology: Descends from Latin mundus ('universe, world, mankind; originally orderly arrangement', calquing Ancient Greek kósmos).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mundo

municipal.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mūnicipālis ('pertaining to a self-governing municipality'), derived from mūnicipium ('town whose citizens assumed civic duties', from mūnia + capere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: municipal

muro.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin mūrus ('city wall, outer stone wall').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: muro

mágico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin magicus, from Ancient Greek magikós ('of the Magi, magical'), derived from mágos ('Persian priestly sage, magician' < Old Persian maguš).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mágico

mãe.etymology: Priberam traces mãe (older madre) to Latin mater, matrem ('mother'), with characteristic Portuguese loss of intervocalic -tr- and nasalization.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mãe

mãe.notes: Plural mães simply adds -s to the nasal diphthong.

mão.etymology: Inherited from Latin manus (accusative manum, 'hand'), via regular loss of intervocalic -n- and nasalization (*mão < mano < manum).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mão

mão.notes: By extension, uma mão de tinta means 'a coat of paint' applied by hand.

métrico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin metricus, from Ancient Greek metrikós ('pertaining to measurement or poetic meter'), derived from métron ('measure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: métrico

mês.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin mēsis, from Classical Latin mēnsis ('month').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mês

móvel.etymology: Descends from Latin mōbilis ('movable, pliable', from movēre 'to move'); substantivized in Portuguese from bens móveis ('movable household chattels') to mean 'piece of furniture'.

history.meaning: to move / movable; piece of furniture

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: móvel

música.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek mousikḗ (tékhnē) ('art of the Muses, lyric poetry and music'), derived from Moûsa ('Muse').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: música

nada.etymology: Inherited from the Vulgar Latin phrase (rēs) nāta ('[any] born or existing thing', feminine past participle of nāscī 'to be born'), which grammaticalized in negative clauses (non ... rem nātam) to mean 'nothing'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nada

naquele.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition em ('in, on' < Old Portuguese en < Latin in) + the distal demonstrative aquele ('that' < Vulgar Latin *eccu(m) ille).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: naquele

nariz.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nārīcae / Late Latin nārīces, an enlarged derivative of Classical Latin nāris, nārēs ('nostril, nose').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nariz

nascer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nāscēre, an active remodeling of the Classical Latin deponent verb nāscī ('to be born, spring forth, arise').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nascer

natural.etymology: Borrowed from Latin nātūrālis ('by birth, according to nature, natural'), derived from nātūra ('birth, nature', from nāscī, nātus 'to be born').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: natural

nem.etymology: Inherited from Latin nec ('and not, nor, not even'), via Old Portuguese nen with progressive nasalization from the initial n-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nem

nenhum.etymology: Inherited from Latin nec ūnus ('not even one, no, none'), via Old Portuguese nengũu / nenhũu.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nenhum

nervoso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nervōsus ('sinewy, vigorous; in modern usage, relating to the nerves, anxious'), derived from nervus ('sinew, tendon, nerve').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nervoso

nessa.etymology: A Portuguese contraction of em and essa, documented as such by Priberam. The combined written word carries both the location relation and the feminine singular demonstrative. It belongs with reunião in this sentence.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nessa

nesse.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition em ('in, on' < Old Portuguese en < Latin in) + the medial masculine demonstrative esse ('that' < Latin ipse).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nesse

neste.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition em ('in, on' < Old Portuguese en < Latin in) + the proximal masculine demonstrative este ('this' < Latin iste).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: neste

neto.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *neptus ('grandson'), a masculine form back-formed from Classical Latin feminine neptis ('granddaughter, niece') that replaced Classical nepōs, nepōtis.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: neto

neve.etymology: Inherited from Latin nix, nivem ('snow'), with regular lowering of short stressed -i- to -e-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: neve

ninguém.etymology: Inherited from Latin nec quem ('not anyone, nobody'), formed in parallel with alguém (< aliquem).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ninguém

nogueira.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nucāria ('walnut tree'), derived from Classical Latin nux, nucis ('walnut, nut'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g- and development of -āria > -eira.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nogueira

noite.etymology: Inherited from Latin nox, noctis (accusative noctem, 'night'), showing the Western Iberian vocalization of -ct- > -it-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: noite

noite.notes: Compare leite (< lactem) and oito (< octō), vs. Spanish noche, leche, ocho.

nome.etymology: Inherited from Latin nōmen, nōminis ('name, appellation, reputation').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nome

nono.etymology: Inherited from Latin nōnus ('ninth'), the ordinal numeral corresponding to novem ('nine').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nono

nos.etymology: Inherited from unstressed Latin accusative/dative nōs ('us, to us').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nos

nossa.etymology: Colloquial exclamation shortened from Nossa Senhora! ('Our Lady!'), where nossa is the feminine of nosso (< Vulgar Latin *nostrus, Classical noster 'our').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nossa

nosso.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nostrus, *nostrum, leveled from Classical Latin noster, nostrum ('our, ours', derived from nōs 'we').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nosso

nota.etymology: Descends from Latin nota ('mark, sign, written character, musical note, grade, banknote').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nota

notícia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nōtitia ('celebrity, acquaintance, knowledge, report, news'), derived from nōtus ('known', past participle of nōscere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: notícia

novata.etymology: Feminine of novato ('newcomer, beginner, novice'), derived in Iberian Romance from novo ('new' < Latin novus) + suffix -ato.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: novata

nove.etymology: Inherited from Latin novem ('nine'), with regular loss of final -m.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nove

novinho.etymology: Diminutive of novo ('new, young' < Latin novus) formed with the suffix -inho, often used intensively for 'brand-new'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: novinho

novo.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin novus ('new, fresh, young').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: novo

num.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition em ('in, on' < Old Portuguese en < Latin in) + the masculine indefinite article um ('a, one' < Latin ūnum).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: num

numa.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition em ('in, on' < Old Portuguese en < Latin in) + the feminine indefinite article uma ('a, one' < Latin ūnam).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: numa

nunca.etymology: Inherited from Latin nunquam / numquam ('never', compounded from ne- 'not' + umquam 'ever').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nunca

não.etymology: The negative word continues Latin non. Priberam distinguishes the ordinary negative adverb from a noun meaning a refusal. This lesson uses negation, including its conversational repetition, rather than the countable noun.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: não

né.etymology: Colloquial Portuguese confirmation particle contracted from the tag question não é? ('isn't it?, right?').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: né

nós.etymology: Inherited from stressed Latin nominative/prepositional nōs ('we, us').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nós

número.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin numerus ('number, count, quantity, rhythm').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: número

o.etymology: Inherited from unstressed Vulgar Latin illum (accusative masculine singular of Classical Latin ille 'that'), via apheresis and regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l- (illu > elo > lo > o).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: o

obrigado.etymology: Originally the past participle of obrigar (< Latin obligāre 'to bind, place under obligation', from ob- + ligāre 'to tie, bind'), grammaticalized from the polite formula fico-lhe obrigado ('I remain obliged/bound to you').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: obrigado

ocupado.etymology: From Latin occupātus ('seized, taken up, busy, occupied'), past participle of occupāre.

history.meaning: to take up, employ / busy, occupied

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ocupado

ocupar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin occupāre ('to take possession of, seize, fill up, employ'), compounded from ob- + capere ('to take, hold').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ocupar

oferecer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *offerēscere, an inchoative remodeling of Classical Latin offerre ('to bring before, present, offer', from ob- + ferre 'to bring').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oferecer

oferecido.etymology: Participial adjective of oferecer ('to offer, present' < Vulgar Latin *offerēscere < Classical Latin offerre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oferecido

oficial.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin officiālis ('pertaining to duty or office; magistrate's official'), derived from Classical Latin officium ('service, duty, office').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oficial

oficialmente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the adjective oficial (< Late Latin officiālis) + adverbial suffix -mente.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oficialmente

oficina.etymology: Descends from Latin officīna ('workshop, manufactory'), contracted in early Latin from *opificīna (derived from opifex 'craftsman, maker', from opus 'work' + facere 'to make').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oficina

oi.etymology: Expressive greeting and attention-calling interjection in Portuguese ('hi!, hey!; pardon?'), developed from a natural vocal call (and reinforced in some dialects by Old Portuguese ouve! 'hear/listen!').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oi

oitava.etymology: Feminine of oitavo, from Latin octāvus ('eighth', from octo 'eight'), showing the regular western Iberian vocalization of -ct- > -it- (octāva > oitava; compare noctem > noite).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oitava

oitava.notes: Marks the eight-step diatonic span from one musical note to the next of the same name.

oitenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *octāgintā (for Classical Latin octōgintā 'eighty', derived from octō 'eight'), with vocalization of preconsonantal -c- (octāgintā > oitaenta > oitenta).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oitenta

oito.etymology: Inherited from Latin octō ('eight'), with regular vocalization of preconsonantal -c- to -i- (octō > oito).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oito

olhada.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from olhar ('to look at') + suffix -ada, denoting a quick look or glance.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: olhada

olhar.etymology: Derived from olho ('eye' < Latin oculus) + verbal suffix -ar (or from Late/Vulgar Latin *oculāre 'to eye, look at').
