porcelana.notes: Used both for fine tableware and for traditional white ceramic electrical fuses.

porque.etymology: Formed in Old Portuguese by fusing the preposition por (< Latin prō / per) + the conjunction/pronoun que (< Latin quid / quod), meaning 'because, for'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: porque

porta.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin porta ('gate, entrance, door').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: porta

portão.etymology: Augmentative of porta ('door, gate' < Latin porta) formed with the suffix -ão, naming a large outer gate or entrance doorway.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: portão

porão.etymology: Formed in Portuguese (originally as a maritime noun naming the lowest cargo hold of a ship, later the basement of a house), derived from pôr ('to put, stow cargo' < Latin pōnere) + augmentative/locative suffix -ão.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: porão

postal.etymology: Borrowed from French postal ('relating to the mail service'), derived from poste (< Italian posta < Latin posita 'stationed relay of horses').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: postal

pote.etymology: Borrowed via Gallo-Romance (Old French pot) from Late Latin pottus ('drinking pot, jar, vessel').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pote

pouco.etymology: Inherited from Latin paucus, paucum ('few, little'), with regular Galician-Portuguese development of Latin au > ou.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pouco

pouquinho.etymology: Diminutive of pouco ('little, a bit' < Latin paucus) formed with the suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pouquinho

pousada.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of pousar ('to stop and rest, lodge' < Late Latin pausāre 'to halt, rest', from pausa < Ancient Greek paûsis 'cessation'), naming a guesthouse or inn.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pousada

pra.etymology: An informal reduced form of para. Priberam also records a Brazilian spelling pra for a contraction including the feminine article a. These are related current uses, not a claim that every spoken pra contains a separately intended article.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pra

pra.notes: Source spelling is preserved. Informal Brazilian pra is not silently expanded in the native dialogue.

prancheta.etymology: Diminutive of prancha ('flat board, plank' < Old French planche < Late Latin planca 'flat slab, board') formed with -eta, naming a drawing board or clipboard.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prancheta

prateado.etymology: Participial adjective of pratear ('to coat with silver, shine like silver'), derived from prata ('silver' < Vulgar Latin *platta [argentea] 'sheet of metal', with rhotacism pl- > pr-).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prateado

prateleira.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from pratel (old diminutive of prato 'plate, dish' < Vulgar Latin *plattus) + suffix -eira, originally a rack for holding dishes and plates, later any shelf.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prateleira

prazer.etymology: Inherited from Latin placēre ('to please, be agreeable'), with Galician-Portuguese rhotacism of initial pl- > pr- and substantivization of the infinitive as 'pleasure'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prazer

praça.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plattea (for Classical Latin platēa 'broad street, courtyard, public square', borrowed from Ancient Greek plateîa [hodós] 'broad way'), with rhotacism pl- > pr-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: praça

precisar.etymology: Derived from preciso ('necessary, exact, indispensable' < Latin praecīsus 'cut off short, definite, exact', past participle of praecīdere 'to cut off in front').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: precisar

prefeitura.etymology: Borrowed from Latin praefectūra ('office or administration of an overseer/prefect', from praefectus, past participle of praeficere 'to place in command'); used in Brazil for the municipal government or city hall.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prefeitura

prender.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin prendere, syncopated form of Classical Latin prehendere ('to lay hold of, grasp, seize, fasten').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prender

preocupar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin praeoccupāre ('to seize beforehand, take possession of the mind in advance'), from prae- ('before') + occupāre ('to occupy, seize').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: preocupar

preparar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin praeparāre ('to make ready beforehand, equip, prepare'), compounded from prae- ('before') + parāre ('to make ready').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: preparar

preso.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin prēsus, reduced from Classical Latin prehēnsus ('seized, caught, fastened'), past participle of prehendere (> prender).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: preso

pressa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin pressa ('pressure, crowding, urgency, haste'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin premere, pressum ('to press hard, urge').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pressa

pressão.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pressiō, pressiōnis ('a pressing down, compression, pressure'), derived from premere, pressum ('to press').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pressão

prestar.etymology: Inherited from Latin praestāre ('to stand before, excel, furnish, render service, be useful', from prae- + stāre 'to stand').

history.meaning: to furnish, render, be of use

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prestar

prestes.etymology: From Old Portuguese preste / prestes ('ready, about to'), inherited from Late Latin praestus ('at hand, ready, prompt', derived from the Classical adverb praestō 'at hand').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prestes

preto.etymology: From Old Portuguese preto ('pressed close, dense, dark, black', a doublet of metathesized perto 'near'), inherited from Late Latin pressus / *prettus ('pressed thick, dense, dark').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: preto

previsão.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval/Modern Latin praevīsiō, praevīsiōnis (reinforced by French prévision), from Latin praevidēre, praevīsum ('to see beforehand, foresee', from prae- + vidēre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: previsão

preço.etymology: Inherited from Latin pretium ('worth, value, price, reward').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: preço

primavera.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra (Classical Latin prīmō vēre, 'at the start of spring'), combining prīmus ('first') and vēr ('spring').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: primavera

primavera.notes: When *verānum (> verão) shifted forward to mean 'summer', *prīma vēra took over the meaning 'spring'.

primeiro.etymology: Inherited from Latin prīmārius ('of the first rank, chief, first'), derived from prīmus ('first'), with regular Galician-Portuguese development of -ārius > -eiro.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: primeiro

primo.etymology: Inherited from the Latin kinship phrase (cōnsobrīnus) prīmus ('first cousin'), from prīmus ('first').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: primo

principal.etymology: Borrowed from Latin prīncipālis ('first in rank, chief, main'), derived from prīnceps, prīncipis ('first, chief', from prīmus 'first' + capere 'to take').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: principal

principalmente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the adjective principal (< Latin prīncipālis) + adverbial suffix -mente.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: principalmente

problema.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek próblēma ('something put forward, obstacle, question proposed for solution', from probállō 'to throw forward').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: problema

procurar.etymology: Descends from Latin prōcūrāre ('to take care of, attend to, endeavor to obtain'), compounded from prō- + cūrāre ('to care for', from cūra 'care').

history.meaning: care / to attend to, seek after

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: procurar

professora.etymology: Feminine of professor, learned borrowing from Latin professor, professōris ('public teacher, one who professes expertise in an art'), from profitērī ('to declare openly').

history.meaning: to declare publicly / public teacher, professor

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: professora

progresso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prōgressus ('a going forward, advance, progress'), derived from prōgredī ('to step forward, advance', from prō- + gradī 'to step').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: progresso

prometer.etymology: Descends from Latin prōmittere ('to send forth, put forward, give one's word, promise'), compounded from prō- ('forth') + mittere ('to send').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prometer

pronto.etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōmptus ('brought forth, ready at hand, prepared, quick'), past participle of prōmere ('to take out, bring forth').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pronto

protegido.etymology: Participial adjective of proteger ('to protect, shield'), from Latin prōtegere ('to cover in front, shelter, defend', from prō- + tegere 'to cover').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: protegido

provador.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from provar ('to taste, test, try on clothes' < Latin probāre) + suffix -dor (< Latin -tōrem / -tōrium), naming both a taster and a shop fitting room.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: provador

provar.etymology: Inherited from Latin probāre ('to test, try, find good, prove, sample'), derived from probus ('good, sound, upright').

history.meaning: to test, prove, taste, try on

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: provar

prédio.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin praedium ('landed estate, urban or rural property'), which specialized in Portuguese for an urban building or apartment block.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: prédio

próprio.etymology: Borrowed from Latin proprius ('one's own, personal, characteristic, proper').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: próprio

próximo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin proximus ('nearest, next, immediately following'), the irregular superlative corresponding to prope ('near').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: próximo

pular.etymology: Inherited from Latin pullāre / pullulāre ('to sprout, spring forth, gambol like a young animal', from pullus 'young animal, foal, chick'), shifting in Portuguese to 'to jump, leap'.

history.meaning: young animal / to spring forth, bound

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pular

puro.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin pūrus ('clean, unmixed, unstained, pure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: puro

puxa.etymology: Colloquial Portuguese exclamation of surprise, admiration, or mild frustration (puxa! / puxa vida! 'gosh!, gee!'), a euphemistic alteration blended with the verb puxar ('to pull, draw out').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: puxa

puxar.etymology: Inherited from Latin pulsāre ('to beat, strike, drive, impel'), frequentative of pellere ('to drive, push'); in Portuguese (likely via maritime hauling of ropes and oars) the sense shifted from 'driving/impelling' to 'pulling'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: puxar

página.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina ('column of writing, leaf or page of a book', originally 'rows of vines fastened together', from pangere 'to fasten').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: página

pálido.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pallidus ('pale, wan, colorless'), derived from pallēre ('to be pale').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pálido

pássaro.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin passarus, a first/second-declension remodeling of Classical Latin passer, passeris ('sparrow'), which generalized in Iberian Romance to any small 'bird'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pássaro

pátio.etymology: Shared with Spanish patio ('inner courtyard, open paved court'), borrowed from Old Occitan/Catalan pati ('open ground, courtyard'), from Late Latin patium / patēre ('to lie open').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pátio

pânico.etymology: Learned borrowing via French panique from Ancient Greek panikós ('of the god Pan, sudden groundless terror attributed to Pan in wild places', from Pán 'Pan').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pânico

pão.etymology: Inherited from Latin pānis (accusative pānem, 'bread, loaf'), via loss of intervocalic -n- and nasalization; plural pães (< pānēs).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pão

pão.notes: Explains why singular -ão (< -ānem) alternates with plural -ães in pão / pães and cão / cães.

pãozinho.etymology: Diminutive of pão ('bread' < Latin pānis, pānem) formed with the suffix -zinho, naming a bread roll.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pãozinho

pé.etymology: Inherited from Latin pēs, pedem ('foot'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -d- (pede > pee > pé).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pé

pôr.etymology: Inherited from Latin pōnere ('to put, place, set down'), via regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -n- and vowel contraction (pōnere > põer > poer > pôr).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pôr

público.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pūblicus ('of the people, belonging to the community, public', altered from Old Latin poplicus, from populus 'people').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: público

quadradinho.etymology: Diminutive of quadrado ('square' < Latin quadrātus) formed with the suffix -inho, meaning 'little square'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quadradinho

quadrado.etymology: Descends from Latin quadrātus ('squared, four-cornered, square'), past participle of quadrāre ('to make square', from quattuor 'four').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quadrado

quadro.etymology: Descends from Latin quadrum ('a square, four-sided figure or frame', related to quattuor 'four'), naming a framed painting, board, or chart.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quadro

qual.etymology: Inherited from Latin quālis, quālem ('of what sort, what kind of, which'), with regular apocope of final -e.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: qual

qualquer.etymology: Compound indefinite determiner/pronoun formed in Romance from qual ('which' < Latin quālis) + quer (third-person singular of querer 'to want, wish' < Latin quaerere), literally 'whichever you will'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: qualquer

quando.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin quandō ('when, at what time').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quando

quanto.etymology: Inherited from Latin quantus, quantum ('how great, how much').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quanto

quarenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin quarranta, reduced from Classical Latin quadrāgintā ('forty', derived from quattuor 'four').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quarenta

quarta.etymology: Short for quarta-feira ('Wednesday', from Ecclesiastical Latin quarta fēria 'fourth liturgical day of the week'), or feminine of quarto (< Latin quarta 'fourth; fourth part').

history.meaning: fourth day of the week, Wednesday; fourth part

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quarta

quarto.etymology: Inherited from Latin quartus ('fourth', ordinal of quattuor 'four'); as a noun, evolved from 'quarter/division of a house' to 'bedroom, room'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quarto

quase.etymology: Learned or semi-learned borrowing from Latin quasi ('as if, just as, nearly, almost').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quase

quatro.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin quattor, reduced from Classical Latin quattuor ('four').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quatro

que.etymology: Inherited from a phonetic convergence of unstressed Latin quid ('what'), quem ('whom'), and quod / quia ('that, because').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: que

quebrado.etymology: Participial adjective of quebrar ('to break' < Vulgar Latin *crepantāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quebrado

quebrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin crepāre ('to rattle, crack, burst') via Vulgar Latin *crepantāre / Old Portuguese crebar, with metathesis of -r- (crebar > quebrar).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quebrar

queijo.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cāseum (Classical Latin cāseus, 'cheese'), via metathesis of the palatal glide and palatalization of -sj- (cāseu > *caisjo > queijo).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: queijo

queimar.etymology: Inherited from Hispano-Latin *caimāre, widely explained as a blend of Classical Latin cremāre ('to burn, consume by fire') with Late Latin cauma ('burning heat' < Ancient Greek kaûma).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: queimar

quem.etymology: Inherited from Latin quem ('whom, who'), accusative singular of the interrogative and relative pronoun quis / quī.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quem

quente.etymology: From Old Portuguese caente, inherited from Latin calēns, calentem ('warm, hot, glowing'), present participle of calēre ('to be warm'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l- (calente > caente > quente).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quente

quentinho.etymology: Diminutive of quente ('warm, hot' < Latin calentem) formed with the suffix -inho, meaning 'pleasantly warm, cozy, fresh from the oven'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quentinho

querer.etymology: Inherited from Latin quaerere ('to seek, look for, ask for, desire'), which shifted in Iberian Romance from 'seeking' to 'wanting, wishing, loving'.

history.meaning: to seek, ask for -> to want, wish

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: querer

querido.etymology: Participial adjective and noun of querer ('to want, love, hold dear' < Latin quaerere), meaning 'dear, beloved, darling'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: querido

quieto.etymology: Learned restoration of Latin quiētus ('at rest, calm, still, quiet', past participle of quiēscere 'to rest'), forming a doublet alongside the inherited popular form quedo.

history.meaning: to rest / at rest, still, quiet

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quieto

quilo.etymology: Shortened form (clipping) of quilograma ('kilogram'), borrowed from French kilo(gramme), coined in 1795 from Ancient Greek khílioi ('a thousand') + grámma ('small weight, gram').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quilo

quinta.etymology: Shortened from quinta-feira, from Late Latin quinta feria ('fifth liturgical day' counting from Sunday), which replaced pagan planetary names in Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quinta

history.meaning: fifth day of the week, Thursday

quinta.notes: Everyday speech routinely shortens quinta-feira to quinta ('na próxima quinta à tarde').

quinze.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quīndece, reduced from Classical Latin quīndecim ('fifteen', compounded from quīnque 'five' + decem 'ten').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quinze

quê.etymology: Stressed tonic form of que, inherited from Latin quid ('what?').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quê

rachado.etymology: Participial adjective of rachar ('to split, crack, cleave').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rachado

rachar.etymology: Shared with Galician rachar ('to split wood, crack, cleave'); derived from a Vulgar Latin or expressive stem for splitting splinters of wood (variously linked to *assulāre 'to splinter' or *radia).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rachar

ramo.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin rāmus ('branch, bough, twig').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ramo

rapidez.etymology: Derived from rápido ('swift, rapid' < Latin rapidus, from rapere 'to seize, sweep along') + abstract noun suffix -ez (< Latin -itiēs).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rapidez

rasgar.etymology: Inherited from Latin resecāre ('to cut back, slit, tear open', from re- + secāre 'to cut'), via syncopated Hispano-Romance *res'gāre > rasgar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rasgar

razão.etymology: Inherited from Latin ratiō, ratiōnem ('reckoning, account, faculty of reason, motive, cause'), derived from rērī, ratus ('to reckon, judge').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: razão

reabertura.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the iterative prefix re- ('again') + abertura ('opening' < Latin apertūra, from aperīre 'to open').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reabertura

reabrir.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the iterative prefix re- ('again' < Latin re-) + abrir ('to open' < Latin aperīre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reabrir

real.etymology: Converges two Latin adjectives: (1) 'royal' (and the name of the historic Portuguese and modern Brazilian currency real), inherited from Latin rēgālis ('royal', from rēx 'king') with loss of intervocalic -g-; (2) 'real, actual', from Medieval Latin reālis (from Classical Latin rēs 'thing, reality').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: real

realmente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the adjective real ('real, actual' < Medieval Latin reālis, from Classical Latin rēs 'thing') + adverbial suffix -mente.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: realmente

recado.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old Portuguese recadar / arrecadar ('to collect, put in safe keeping, deliver a commission' < Vulgar Latin *recapitāre, derived from caput 'head'), naming a message or errand.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: recado

receber.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *recipēre (for Classical Latin recipere 'to take back, receive, welcome', from re- + capere 'to take'), with voicing of intervocalic -p- to -b-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: receber

recepcionista.etymology: Derived from recepção ('reception, front desk' < Latin receptiō) + occupational suffix -ista (modeled on French réceptionniste / English receptionist).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: recepcionista

recepção.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin receptiō, receptiōnis ('a receiving, admission, welcome, shelter'), derived from recipere, receptum ('to receive').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: recepção

recibo.etymology: Borrowed from Spanish recibo (or Medieval administrative practice where a payment acknowledgment began with recibo 'I receive', from Latin recipiō), naming a written receipt.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: recibo

reconhecer.etymology: Inherited from Latin recognōscere ('to know again, recall to mind, examine, recognize'), compounded from re- + cognōscere ('to come to know').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reconhecer

recuperar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin recuperāre ('to get back, regain, recover, restore').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: recuperar

recusar.etymology: Borrowed or inherited from Latin recūsāre ('to make an objection against, decline, refuse, reject', built on re- + causa 'cause, pretext').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: recusar

redondo.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin retundus, dissimilated from Classical Latin rotundus ('wheel-shaped, round, circular', derived from rota 'wheel'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: redondo

reencontro.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from iterative prefix re- ('again') + encontro ('meeting, encounter', deverbal from encontrar < Late Latin incontrāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reencontro

registrado.etymology: Participial adjective of registrar ('to record in a register, log' < Medieval Latin registrāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: registrado

registro.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin registrum (altered from Late Latin regesta 'things recorded, list, register', neuter plural past participle of Classical Latin regerere 'to transcribe, record'); in Brazil, also names a water or gas shut-off valve.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: registro

região.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin regiō, regiōnis ('direction, boundary line, district, region'), derived from regere ('to direct, rule, draw a line').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: região

regra.etymology: Inherited from Latin rēgula ('straight stick, ruler, pattern, rule', derived from regere 'to guide straight, rule'), via syncope and rhotacism (rēg'la > regra).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: regra

relojoeiro.etymology: Derived from relógio ('clock, watch' < Latin hōrologium < Ancient Greek hōrológion 'hour-teller', via Old Spanish/Catalan stem reloj-) + occupational suffix -eiro (< Latin -ārius).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: relojoeiro

relâmpago.etymology: From Old Portuguese relampado / relâmpago, derived from Vulgar Latin *relampāre ('to flash brightly', from re- + lampas, lampadis 'torch, lightning flash' < Ancient Greek lampás).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: relâmpago

relógio.etymology: From Latin horolŏgium ('sundial, water clock'), borrowed from Greek hōrológion ('hour-indicator', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: relógio

relógio.notes: Covers wall clocks, tower clocks, and wristwatches (relógio de pulso).

renda.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rendita ('that which is yielded back, income, revenue, rent'), feminine past participle of *rendere (Classical reddere 'to give back, yield', nasalized by analogy with prendere); also used in Portuguese for decorative 'lace'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: renda

repetir.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned adaptation from Latin repetere ('to seek again, return to, repeat'), composed of re- ('again') and petere ('to seek, aim at').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: repetir

reserva.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Portuguese from reservar ('to keep back, set aside, reserve').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reserva

reservar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin reservāre ('to keep back, save up, preserve'), from re- ('back') and servāre ('to keep, guard, preserve').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reservar

resolver.etymology: Borrowed from Latin resolvere ('to untie, loosen, melt, resolve'), composed of re- ('back, again') and solvere ('to loosen, release').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: resolver

respeitar.etymology: Formed from respeito ('respect') + -ar, or adapted from Latin respectāre ('to look back at, regard with care'), frequentative of respicere.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: respeitar

respirar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin respīrāre ('to breathe out, catch one's breath, breathe'), composed of re- ('back, again') and spīrāre ('to breathe, blow').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: respirar

restar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin restāre ('to stay behind, stand firm, remain'), composed of re- ('back, behind') and stāre ('to stand').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: restar

reto.etymology: Borrowed from Latin rēctus ('straight, upright, direct'), past participle of regere ('to guide, direct, rule'), with reduction of the cluster -ct- to -t-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reto

reunião.etymology: Priberam analyses reunião as re- plus união. The modern noun names the act of gathering or a gathering of people; a workplace meeting is one application of that meaning. The plural changes to reuniões.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reunião

rico.etymology: Borrowed from Gothic reiks ('ruler, mighty, powerful') or a related West Germanic cognate (*rīkijaz, 'powerful, wealthy'), which entered Western Romance during the early medieval period.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rico

rio.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin rīus, from Classical Latin rīvus ('stream, brook, water channel').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rio

ripa.etymology: Of debated origin; usually traced either to a Germanic word meaning 'rib, narrow strip of wood' (compare Middle Low German rippe, Old High German rippa) or to Latin rīpa ('bank, edge, border').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ripa

rir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rīdīre, a fourth-conjugation remodeling of Classical Latin rīdēre ('to laugh'), with regular loss of intervocalic -d- and vowel contraction.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rir

ritmo.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin rhythmus from Greek rhythmós ('measured flow, recurring beat'), related to rheîn ('to flow').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ritmo

ritmo.notes: In Brazilian speech, an epenthetic vowel softens the -tm- cluster ([ˈʁitʃimu]).

rodinha.etymology: Formed in Portuguese as the diminutive of roda ('wheel, circle' < Latin rota) + the diminutive suffix -inha.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rodinha

rodoviária.etymology: Ellipsis of estação rodoviária ('highway bus station'), feminine of rodoviário, formed in Portuguese from roda ('wheel' < Latin rota) + via ('road, way' < Latin via) + -ária.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rodoviária

rolo.etymology: Inherited from Latin rotulus ('little wheel, cylinder, scroll'), diminutive of rota ('wheel'), via Vulgar Latin *rotlus.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rolo

rosca.etymology: Of uncertain pre-Roman Iberian origin (shared with Spanish rosca and Galician rosca), denoting a spiral coil, screw thread, or ring-shaped bread.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rosca

roupa.etymology: Derived from Germanic (Gothic *raupa or West Germanic *rauba, 'spoils, booty, garments stripped from a defeated enemy', from the same root as roubar 'to rob').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: roupa

rua.etymology: From Late Latin rūga ('lined street, path bordered by houses', originally 'wrinkle, crease, furrow' in Classical Latin), either directly or reinforced by Old French rue.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rua

ruim.etymology: Inherited from Latin ruīna ('downfall, collapse, ruin', from ruere 'to fall, rush down'), which came to be used in Old Portuguese (roim) as an adjective meaning 'wretched, bad, of poor quality'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ruim

ruído.etymology: Inherited from Latin rugītus ('roaring, rumbling', from rugīre 'to roar, rumble'), with regular loss of intervocalic -g-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ruído

rá.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection representing a sudden burst of laughter, triumph, or playful mockery ('ha!').

history.meaning: expressive exclamation of laughter or surprise

sources.title: Wiktionary: rá

rápido.etymology: Borrowed from Latin rapidus ('seizing, tearing away, swift, rapid'), derived from rapere ('to seize, snatch, carry off').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: rápido

ré.etymology: In the directional and automotive sense ('stern, reverse gear', as in dar ré or marcha à ré), derived via Old Portuguese rês / Old Occitan or Catalan rere from Latin retrō ('backward, behind').

history.meaning: stern of a ship; backward motion, reverse

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ré

régua.etymology: Semi-popular reflex of Latin regŭla ('straight wooden strip, ruler'), derived from regĕre ('to guide straight').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: régua

régua.notes: Portuguese split Latin regŭla into two everyday words: régua ('measuring ruler') and regra ('rule, regulation').

saber.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Classical Latin sapere ('to taste, have good taste, discern, be wise, know'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -p- to -b-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: saber

sabonete.etymology: Adapted from French savonnette ('scented toilet soap', diminutive of savon 'soap'), reshaped after Portuguese sabão (< Latin sāpōnem).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sabonete

sabão.etymology: From Late Latin sapōnem (nominative sapo, 'soap'), an early Germanic loanword (*saipō) adopted into Latin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sabão

sabão.notes: Regularly turned Latin -ōnem into Portuguese -ão and voiced intervocalic -p- to -b-.

sacola.etymology: Borrowed from Italian saccola ('small bag, pouch') or formed in Portuguese from saco ('bag, sack' < Latin saccus) + diminutive/nominal suffix -ola.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sacola

sair.etymology: Inherited from Latin salīre ('to leap, jump, bound forth'), which shifted in Iberian Romance to mean 'to go out, exit', with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sair
Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sal

sala.etymology: Derived from Germanic *sal- ('hall, large single-room dwelling'; compare Old High German sal, Frankish *sal), transmitted through Late Latin sala or Old French sale.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sala

salvar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin salvāre ('to save, rescue, deliver'), derived from Classical Latin salvus ('safe, whole, unharmed').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: salvar

salvo.etymology: Inherited from Latin salvus ('safe, whole, unharmed, preserved').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: salvo

sapato.etymology: Of uncertain ultimate origin; shared with Spanish zapato and usually traced to Andalusi Arabic sabbāṭ ('leather shoe, footwear') or a pre-Roman Iberian / Eurasian wanderwort.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sapato

saudade.etymology: Inherited from Latin sōlitātem (accusative of sōlitās, 'loneliness, solitude', from sōlus 'alone'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese soidade and suidade with phonological remodeling influenced by saúde ('health') and saudar ('to greet').

history.meaning: solitude, longing for an absent person or place

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: saudade

se.etymology: As a conditional conjunction ('if, whether'), inherited from Latin sī ('if') via unstressed Vulgar Latin se; as a reflexive pronoun ('oneself, themselves'), inherited from Latin sē.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: se

secar.etymology: Inherited from Latin siccāre ('to dry, make dry, drain'), derived from siccus ('dry').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: secar

seco.etymology: Inherited from Latin siccus ('dry, parched, thirsty'), with degemination of -cc- to -c-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: seco

secreto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin sēcrētus ('set apart, hidden, concealed, secret'), past participle of sēcernere ('to separate, set apart', from sē- 'apart' + cernere 'to sift, distinguish'); a doublet of inherited segredo.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: secreto

segredo.etymology: Inherited from Latin sēcrētum ('isolated place, mystery, secret', neuter past participle of sēcernere 'to set apart'), with regular Western Iberian voicing of -cr- to -gr- and intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: segredo

seguinte.etymology: Derived from seguir ('to follow') + participial suffix -nte, continuing Latin sequentem (accusative present participle of sequī 'to follow') remodeled after the verb stem.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: seguinte

seguir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sequīre, regularized from Classical Latin deponent sequī ('to follow, accompany').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: seguir

segunda.etymology: Ellipsis of segunda-feira ('Monday'), or the feminine form of segundo ('second'), inherited from Latin secunda (feminine of secundus, 'following, second').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: segunda

segunda-feira.etymology: Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin secunda fēria ('second liturgical day after Sunday'), promoted in 6th-century Gallaecia by Bishop Martin of Braga to replace the pagan Roman name diēs Lūnae ('day of the Moon').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: segunda-feira

segundo.etymology: Inherited from Latin secundus ('following, next, second', from sequī 'to follow'), with intervocalic voicing of -c- to -g-; as a unit of time, from Medieval Latin pars minūta secunda ('second small division' of an hour).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: segundo

segurança.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from segurar ('to secure, hold fast') or seguro ('safe') + the abstract noun suffix -ança.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: segurança

segurar.etymology: Derived from seguro ('safe, firm, secure' < Latin sēcūrus) + verbal suffix -ar, developing in Portuguese the concrete sense 'to hold, grip firmly'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: segurar

seguro.etymology: Inherited from Latin sēcūrus ('free from care, untroubled, safe', composed of sē- 'without' and cūra 'care, worry'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: seguro

seis.etymology: Inherited from Latin sex ('six'), with vocalization of the velar consonant in the cluster -ks- to -is.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: seis

sem.etymology: Inherited from Latin sine ('without'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese sen to modern sem.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sem

semana.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin septimāna ('week, period of seven days'), noun use of Classical Latin septimānus ('pertaining to the number seven', from septem 'seven').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: semana

sempre.etymology: Inherited from Latin semper ('always, at all times, ever'), with regular Romance metathesis of final -er to -re.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sempre

senhor.etymology: Inherited from Latin seniōrem (accusative of senior, 'older, elder', comparative of senex 'old'), which came to mean 'lord, master' in feudal and courtly usage.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: senhor

senhora.etymology: Feminine form of senhor (< Latin seniōrem 'elder, lord'), created by adding the feminine ending -a to originally two-gender Old Galician-Portuguese senhor.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: senhora

sentado.etymology: Past participle of sentar ('to sit, seat'), used adjectivally ('seated, sitting').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sentado

sentar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sedentāre (built on Classical Latin sedentem, present participle of sedēre 'to sit'), or extracted by apheresis from assentar (< *adsedentāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sentar

sentimental.etymology: Derived from sentimento ('feeling, sentiment' < sentir) + -al, modeled on French sentimental (which was itself coined in 18th-century English as sentimental).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sentimental

sentir.etymology: Inherited from Latin sentīre ('to perceive by the senses, feel, experience, think').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sentir

senão.etymology: Univerbation formed in Portuguese from the conditional conjunction se ('if' < Latin sī) and the negation adverb não ('not' < Latin nōn), literally 'if not'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: senão

sequinho.etymology: Diminutive of seco ('dry' < Latin siccus) + the diminutive suffix -inho, with regular orthographic change of c to qu before i.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sequinho

ser.etymology: Priberam records Latin sedeo, -ere, meaning to sit, in the history of ser. This is not an explanation that every modern form comes regularly from a single written stem: the modern verb is irregular, including sou and é in this exchange.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ser

serra.etymology: Inherited from Latin serra ('saw'), extended metaphorically in Iberian Romance to a jagged mountain range whose peaks resemble the teeth of a saw.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: serra

servir.etymology: Inherited from Latin servīre ('to be a servant or slave, serve, be useful to'), derived from servus ('slave, servant').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: servir

serviço.etymology: Inherited or semi-learned adaptation from Latin servitium ('condition of a servant, service, duty'), derived from servus ('servant, slave').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: serviço

seta.etymology: Inherited from Latin sagitta ('arrow, shaft'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese saeta and seeta via loss of intervocalic -g- and vowel contraction.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: seta

sete.etymology: Inherited from Latin septem ('seven'), with assimilation of the cluster -pt- to -t- and loss of final -m.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sete

setor.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin sector, sectōris ('cutter; geometric sector of a circle', from secāre 'to cut'), reinforced in modern administrative senses by French secteur.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: setor

seu.etymology: Inherited from Latin suus, suum ('his, her, its, their own'), remodeled in Vulgar Latin on the pattern of meus ('my') to yield Old Galician-Portuguese seu.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: seu

sexta.etymology: Ellipsis of sexta-feira ('Friday'), or the feminine form of sexto ('sixth'), inherited from Latin sexta (feminine of sextus 'sixth', from sex 'six').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sexta

sexta-feira.etymology: Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin sexta fēria ('sixth liturgical day after Sunday'), adopted in early medieval Portuguese Christian usage in place of Roman diēs Veneris ('day of Venus').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sexta-feira

silencioso.etymology: Borrowed from Latin silentiōsus ('full of silence, perfectly still'), derived from silentium ('silence').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: silencioso

silêncio.etymology: Borrowed from Latin silentium ('noiselessness, stillness, silence'), derived from silēre ('to be noiseless or still').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: silêncio

sim.etymology: Inherited from Latin sīc ('so, thus', used in affirmative answers such as sīc est 'so it is'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese si and acquiring final nasalization (sim) by analogy with its antonym não ('no').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sim

simples.etymology: Adapted from Latin simplex, simplicis ('single, plain, uncompounded, simple', from *sem- 'one' + *plek- 'to fold'), with final -s generalized from the plural or old singular nominative.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: simples

simplesmente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from simples ('simple, plain') + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin mente, ablative of mēns 'mind, manner').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: simplesmente

simpático.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin sympathicus, from Ancient Greek συμπαθής (sympathḗs, 'having fellow feeling, congenial, sympathetic'), composed of σύν (sýn, 'with') and πάθος (páthos, 'feeling, emotion').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: simpático

sinceramente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from sincera (feminine of sincero, 'sincere') + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin mente, ablative of mēns 'mind').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sinceramente

sinceridade.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin sincēritātem (accusative of sincēritās, 'purity, integrity, candor, sincerity'), derived from sincērus ('pure, genuine, sincere').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sinceridade

sincero.etymology: Borrowed from Latin sincērus ('clean, pure, whole, unspoiled, genuine, sincere').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sincero

sino.etymology: Inherited from Latin signum ('mark, token, signal'), which in Medieval ecclesiastical Latin came to designate a church bell rung to give liturgical signals.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sino

soar.etymology: Inherited from Latin sonāre ('to sound, resound, make a noise', from sonus 'sound'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -n- (sõar > soar).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: soar

sob.etymology: Inherited from Latin sub ('under, beneath, below').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sob

sobrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin superāre ('to rise above, surmount, exceed, be in abundance, be left over', from super 'above, over'), with voicing of -p- to -b- and syncope of the unstressed vowel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sobrar

sobre.etymology: Inherited from Latin super ('above, over, upon, concerning'), with regular voicing of -p- to -b- and metathesis of final -er to -re.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sobre

sobreviver.etymology: Formed from sobre- ('over, beyond') + viver ('to live'), continuing Late Latin supervīvere ('to outlive, survive', from super + vīvere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sobreviver

sol.etymology: Inherited from Latin sōl, sōlis ('the sun, sunlight').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sol

soleira.etymology: Derived from solo ('ground, floor' < Latin solum) or sola ('sole, bottom sill' < Late Latin sola) + the suffix -eira (compare Vulgar Latin *solāria, 'threshold beam').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: soleira

soltar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *soltāre (contracted from *solutāre), a frequentative verb formed on Classical Latin solūtus ('loosened, untied, free'), past participle of solvere ('to loosen, untie').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: soltar

som.etymology: Inherited from Latin sonum (accusative of sonus, 'sound, noise, tone'), with apocope of the final vowel and nasalization of the vowel before final -n/-m.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: som

sombra.etymology: Priberam traces sombra to Latin subumbra / umbra ('shade, shadow'), shared with Spanish sombra.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sombra

sombra.notes: Covers both welcome shade under a tree (na sombra) and a dark silhouette (aquela sombra).

sonhar.etymology: Inherited from Latin somniāre ('to dream', derived from somnium 'dream'), with palatalization of the cluster -mni- to -nh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sonhar

sonho.etymology: Inherited from Latin somnium ('dream, vision in sleep', derived from somnus 'sleep'), with palatalization of -mni- to -nh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sonho

sono.etymology: Inherited from Latin somnum (accusative of somnus, 'sleep, slumber'), with assimilation of the cluster -mn- to -n-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sono

sopa.etymology: Derived from Germanic *suppa ('slice of bread soaked in broth, sop'), entering Portuguese via Late Latin suppa or Old French soupe.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sopa

soprar.etymology: Inherited from Latin sufflāre ('to blow up from below, puff, inflate', from sub- 'under' + flāre 'to blow'), with regular Western Iberian shift of post-consonantal -fl- to -pr-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: soprar

sorrir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subrīdīre, remodeled from Classical Latin subrīdēre ('to smile', literally 'to laugh slightly or quietly', from sub- 'under, slightly' + rīdēre 'to laugh').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sorrir

sorriso.etymology: Derived from Late/Vulgar Latin *subrīsus ('smile', formed from subrīdēre on the model of rīsus 'laughter'), or formed in Portuguese alongside sorrir.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sorriso

sorte.etymology: Inherited from Latin sortem (accusative of sors, 'lot drawn in divination, share, destiny, fortune, chance').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sorte

sovar.etymology: Probably inherited from a Vulgar Latin *subāre reduced from Classical Latin subigere ('to work under the hands, knead dough, press down, tame', from sub- + agere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sovar

sozinho.etymology: Formed in Portuguese as the diminutive of só ('alone, single' < Latin sōlus) + the linking consonant -z- + diminutive suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sozinho

suave.etymology: Borrowed from Latin suāvis ('sweet, pleasant, agreeable, gentle to the senses').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: suave

suavizar.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from suave ('gentle, soft, mild' < Latin suāvis) + the verbal suffix -izar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: suavizar

subir.etymology: Inherited from Latin subīre ('to go under, approach from below, mount, ascend, climb', composed of sub- 'under, from below' and īre 'to go').

history.meaning: to go from below, mount, climb

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: subir

suco.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin sūcus ('juice, sap, natural moisture of plants or bodies', doublet of inherited sumo).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: suco

sul.etymology: Borrowed from Old French sud / sur (itself from Old English sūþ < Proto-Germanic *sunþaz 'south'), with adaptation of the final consonant to -l in Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sul

sumir.etymology: Inherited from Latin sūmere ('to take up, consume, swallow up', shifted to the -ir conjugation as *sūmīre and influenced by consumir), which developed in Iberian Romance the intransitive sense 'to sink out of sight, vanish, disappear'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sumir

surpreso.etymology: Adapted from French surpris ('surprised', past participle of surprendre 'to overtake, surprise'), reshaped after Portuguese preso ('caught, seized' < Latin prehēnsus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: surpreso

susto.etymology: Back-formation from assustar ('to frighten, startle'), which is usually traced to Latin suscitāre ('to rouse up, awaken suddenly, startle') or an expressive Romance formation.

history.meaning: to rouse, stir up, awaken suddenly

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: susto

sábado.etymology: Priberam traces sábado through Late Latin sabbatum and Greek sábbaton to Hebrew šabbāṯ ('day of rest').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sábado

sábado.notes: With domingo, sábado is one of the two weekend days that do not use -feira in Portuguese.

são.etymology: As an adjective ('healthy, sound, whole'), inherited from Latin sānus ('sound, healthy') via regular loss of intervocalic -n- (Old Portuguese são).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: são

sério.etymology: Borrowed from Latin sērius ('grave, earnest, serious, no-nonsense').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sério

só.etymology: Inherited from Latin sōlus ('alone, single, only'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese soo (with regular loss of intervocalic -l-) and vowel contraction to só.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: só

sócio.etymology: Borrowed from Latin socius ('companion, comrade, ally, partner, business associate').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sócio

sótão.etymology: Traced either to Arabic suṭūḥ (plural of saṭḥ, 'roof, upper terrace') or to Vulgar Latin *subtānus ('lower room, cellar' < subtus 'under', compare Spanish sótano), with a shift in Portuguese architectural usage to the room directly under the roof ('attic, garret').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sótão

tabela.etymology: Borrowed from Latin tabella ('small board, writing tablet, game board, list'), diminutive of tabula ('board, plank, tablet').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tabela

tablet.etymology: Borrowed from English tablet (short for tablet computer), itself from Old French tablete ('small flat slab or writing tablet'), diminutive of table (< Latin tabula 'board, tablet').

history.meaning: small flat slab, writing pad; tablet computer

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tablet

talvez.etymology: Univerbation formed in Portuguese from tal ('such' < Latin tālis) and vez ('time, occasion' < Latin vicis), literally 'at such a time, on some occasion', whence 'perhaps, maybe'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: talvez

tamanho.etymology: Inherited from the Latin phrase tam magnus ('so great, as large as'), fused into a single word with regular palatalization of -gn- to -nh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tamanho

também.etymology: Univerbation formed in Old Galician-Portuguese from tan / tão ('so, as' < Latin tam) and bem ('well' < Latin bene), literally 'equally well, also, too'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: também

tampa.etymology: Deverbal noun from tampar ('to cover with a lid') or variant of tapa ('lid, cover'), derived from Germanic *tappo ('plug, stopper, bung') with nasal epenthesis.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tampa

tanto.etymology: Inherited from Latin tantus, tantum ('of such size, so great, so much').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tanto

tapete.etymology: Borrowed from Latin tapēte ('carpet, rug, tapestry'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τάπης, τάπητος (tápēs, tápētos, 'carpet, woven rug').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tapete

tarde.etymology: Inherited from Latin tardē ('slowly, late', adverb of tardus 'slow, tardy, late'), nominalized in Iberian Romance (compare hora tarde) to designate the afternoon.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tarde

tarefa.etymology: From Arabic ṭarīḥa ('piece of work assigned to be finished within a given time'), derived from ṭaraḥa ('to cast, set before').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tarefa

tarefa.notes: Portuguese preserved Arabic -f- (< pharyngeal -ḥ- adapted as labiodental -f-) where Spanish lost it (tarea).

tchau.etymology: Borrowed from Italian ciao ('hello, goodbye'), originally a Venetian courtly greeting s-ciavo / s-ciao ('[I am your] servant', from Medieval Latin sclāvus 'Slav, slave').

history.meaning: your servant -> informal greeting or farewell

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tchau

te.etymology: Inherited from Latin tē, accusative and ablative singular of the second-person pronoun tū ('you, thee').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: te

tecla.etymology: Shared with Spanish tecla ('key of a musical instrument or keyboard'), of uncertain ultimate origin; often tentatively linked to Latin tēgula ('small flat tile or strip of wood') or Late Latin thecla.

history.meaning: lever or key of an organ or keyboard

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tecla

teimosia.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from teimoso ('stubborn, obstinate') + the abstract noun suffix -ia.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: teimosia

teimoso.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from teima ('persistent fixation, stubbornness', altered from Late Latin thema < Ancient Greek θέμα 'proposition, theme, fixed topic') + the adjectival suffix -oso.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: teimoso

tela.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned adaptation from Latin tēla ('woven fabric, web, canvas', from the root of texere 'to weave'; doublet of inherited teia), later extended to 'painting canvas' and 'screen'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tela

telefone.etymology: Borrowed from French téléphone, an international scientific compound formed from Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, 'far off, at a distance') and φωνή (phōnḗ, 'voice, sound').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: telefone

telefonema.etymology: Coined in Portuguese from telefonar / telefone ('telephone') + the Greek-derived resultative noun suffix -ema (on the model of telegrama 'telegram').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: telefonema

telhado.etymology: From Latin tegulātum ('tiled roof') or formed from telha ('roof tile', < Latin tegŭla, from tegĕre 'to cover') + -ado.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: telhado

telhado.notes: Distinguished in Portuguese from o teto ('indoor ceiling', < Latin tectum).

tempestade.etymology: From Latin tempestātem (nominative tempestas, 'season, weather, storm'), derived from tempus ('time, weather condition').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tempestade

tempestade.notes: Illustrates how o tempo in Romance languages still means both 'time' and 'weather'.

tempo.etymology: Inherited from Latin tempus ('time, period, season, weather condition').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tempo

tentar.etymology: Inherited or adapted from Latin tentāre (variant of temptāre, 'to feel, touch, test, try, attempt').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tentar

ter.etymology: Inherited from Latin tenēre ('to hold, keep, possess'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese teer and tẽer via regular loss of intervocalic -n- and vowel contraction.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ter

terceiro.etymology: Inherited from Latin tertiārius ('containing a third part, third'), derived from tertius ('third', from trēs 'three').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: terceiro

terminar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin termināre ('to set bounds to, limit, bring to an end, finish'), derived from terminus ('boundary stone, limit, end').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: terminar

terça.etymology: Ellipsis of terça-feira ('Tuesday'), or the feminine form of terço ('third'), inherited from Latin tertia (feminine of tertius 'third').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: terça

terça-feira.etymology: Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin tertia fēria ('third liturgical day after Sunday'), adopted in early Portuguese Christian usage to replace Roman diēs Mārtis ('day of Mars').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: terça-feira

testa.etymology: Inherited from Latin testa ('baked clay pot, tile, shell'), used colloquially in Late Latin for 'skull, head' and narrowed in Portuguese (and Italian) to 'forehead, front'.

history.meaning: earthen pot, shell; (Late Latin) skull, head

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: testa

testar.etymology: In the sense 'to put to a test, try out', derived from teste ('test' < English test < Old French test < Latin testum 'earthen cupel used to assay metals') or borrowed from French tester; in the legal sense 'to make a will', from Latin testārī.

history.meaning: assaying vessel / to bear witness, make a will

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: testar

teto.etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned adaptation from Latin tēctum ('roof, ceiling, shelter', neuter past participle of tegere 'to cover'), with simplification of -ct- to -t-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: teto

teu.etymology: Inherited from Latin tuus, tuum ('your, thy'), remodeled in Vulgar Latin on the vowel pattern of meus ('my') to yield Old Galician-Portuguese teu.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: teu

tia.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin thia ('aunt'), borrowed from Ancient Greek θεία (theía, 'aunt', feminine of θεῖος).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tia

tigela.etymology: Priberam derives tigela from Latin tegillum / Late Latin tegella (diminutive linked to tegere, 'to cover'), applied to a small earthenware vessel or bowl.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tigela

history.meaning: small cover; small earthen pan or bowl

tigela.notes: Standard everyday word in Brazil for a soup, cereal, or mixing bowl.

tijolo.etymology: Derived from Late Latin *tegēŏlum (diminutive of Classical Latin tēgula 'roof tile, baked clay tile', from tegere 'to cover'), transmitted through Mozarabic or Old Spanish tejuelo.

history.meaning: baked clay tile -> small tile, brick

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tijolo

tinta.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin tincta ('dyed liquid, pigment, ink', feminine of Classical Latin tinctus, past participle of tingere 'to dip, moisten, dye').

history.meaning: to dye, stain -> dyed liquid, ink, paint

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tinta

tio.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin thius ('uncle'), borrowed from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos, 'uncle', originally 'divine, revered').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tio

tipo.etymology: Borrowed from Latin typus ('figure, image, model, pattern'), from Ancient Greek τύπος (týpos, 'blow, impression, mark, model, type', from τύπτειν 'to strike').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tipo

tirar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre ('to draw, pull, remove', shared with Spanish tirar, French tirer, and Italian tirare), of debated ultimate origin (variously linked to Germanic *tēran 'to tear, pull' or Latin trahere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tirar

toa.etymology: Originally a nautical term meaning 'towrope' (preserved chiefly in the idiom à toa, 'in tow, adrift, aimlessly, for nothing'); borrowed via Old French toue from Old Norse tog or Old English toge ('rope for pulling, tow').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: toa

toalha.etymology: Borrowed via Old Occitan toalha (or Old French touaille) from Frankish *þwahlja ('wash-cloth, towel', derived from Proto-Germanic *þwahaną 'to wash').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: toalha

tocar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *toccāre ('to knock, strike a bell, touch', shared with Spanish tocar, French toucher, and Italian toccare), of expressive onomatopoeic origin (*tok-, imitating a tap or knock).

history.meaning: to knock, tap, strike a bell, touch
to touch, ring, play an instrument

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tocar

todo.etymology: Inherited from Latin tōtus, tōtum ('all, whole, entire'), with regular Western Iberian voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: todo

tom.etymology: Inherited or adapted from Latin tonus ('tension of a cord, pitch, tone, accent'), borrowed from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, 'stretching, taut string, pitch', from τείνειν 'to stretch').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tom

tomar.etymology: Characteristic Ibero-Romance verb (shared with Spanish tomar) of uncertain ultimate origin; variously traced to Latin autumāre ('to affirm, reckon'), a Vulgar Latin *tumbāre, or a pre-Roman substrate root.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tomar

tomate.etymology: Entered Portuguese via Spanish tomate from Classical Nahuatl tomatl ('plump fruit, tomatillo').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tomate

tomate.notes: Became a cornerstone of both Iberian and Brazilian cooking from the 16th–17th centuries onward.

toque.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Portuguese from tocar ('to touch, tap, ring, play an instrument').

history.meaning: to touch, ring -> touch, tap, ring, musical note

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: toque

torcer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torcēre, remodeled from Classical Latin torquēre ('to twist, wind, wring, bend').

history.meaning: to twist, wring; (later) to root for a team

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: torcer

torneira.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from torno ('lathe, swivel, wooden spigot' < Latin tornus < Ancient Greek τόρνος 'lathe, circular tool') + the instrumental suffix -eira.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: torneira

tornozelo.etymology: Formed from Old Portuguese torno ('pivot, rounded projection, anklebone' < Latin tornus) + the diminutive suffix -zelo (< Latin -icellus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tornozelo

torrada.etymology: Nominalized feminine past participle of torrar ('to toast, roast, parch' < Latin torrēre 'to dry up, parch, roast').

history.meaning: to toast -> slice of toasted bread, toast

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: torrada

torta.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin tōrta (pānis) ('twisted or round loaf of bread, tart, pastry', feminine past participle of Classical Latin torquēre 'to twist, wind').

history.meaning: twisted or rolled loaf, round pastry

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: torta

tortinha.etymology: Formed in Portuguese as the diminutive of torta ('pie, tart' < Late Latin tōrta) + the diminutive suffix -inha.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tortinha

torção.etymology: Borrowed or adapted from Late Latin torsiōnem / tortiōnem (accusative of torsiō, 'twisting, wringing, sprain', derived from torquēre 'to twist').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: torção

total.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin tōtālis ('whole, entire, complete'), derived from Classical Latin tōtus ('all, whole').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: total

totalmente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from total ('whole, complete') + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin mente, ablative of mēns 'mind, manner').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: totalmente

trabalhar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre ('to torture with the tripālium; to suffer, toil, labor'), derived from Late Latin tripālium ('instrument of torture made of three stakes', from trēs 'three' + pālus 'stake').

history.meaning: three-staked frame -> to torment, toil, labor

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trabalhar

trabalho.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from trabalhar ('to toil, work' < Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trabalho

trancado.etymology: Past participle of trancar ('to bar, bolt, lock'), used adjectivally ('locked, barred, shut tight').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trancado

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trancar

tranquilo.etymology: Borrowed from Latin tranquillus ('calm, still, quiet, serene, untroubled').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tranquilo

transformar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin trānsformāre ('to change in shape, metamorphose, transform'), composed of trāns- ('across, beyond') and formāre ('to shape, fashion', from forma 'form, shape').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: transformar

trava.etymology: Deverbal noun from travar ('to fetter, lock, brake'), or a feminine variant of trave ('wooden beam, bar' < Latin trabem, accusative of trabs 'beam, timber').

history.meaning: to lock, brake -> latch, catch, lock

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trava

travar.etymology: Formed in Old Galician-Portuguese from trave / trava ('wooden beam, hobble or fetter placed on an animal's legs' < Latin trabs, trabem 'beam, timber') + the verbal suffix -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: travar

travesseiro.etymology: Derived from travesso ('placed across, transverse' < Latin trānsversus) + the suffix -eiro (compare Late Latin *trānsversārius), originally naming a long bolster pillow laid across the full width of the bed.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: travesseiro

trazer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tragere, remodeled from Classical Latin trahere ('to draw, drag, pull, bring'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese trager to modern trazer.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trazer

trem.etymology: Borrowed from French train ('retinue, line of vehicles, railway train'), derived from Old French traïner ('to drag, draw along' < Vulgar Latin *tragīnāre, from Latin trahere 'to draw, pull').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trem

tremer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tremēre, a second-conjugation shift of Classical Latin tremere ('to shake, quake, tremble, quiver').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tremer

trenzinho.etymology: Formed in Portuguese as the diminutive of trem ('train' < French train) + the linking consonant -z- + diminutive suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trenzinho

trinco.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from trincar ('to snap, bite, click shut'), of expressive onomatopoeic origin (*trink-, imitating the sharp metallic click of a door latch).

history.meaning: to click, snap -> door latch, catch

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trinco

trinta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīnta, contracted from Classical Latin trīgintā ('thirty').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trinta

triste.etymology: Inherited or adapted from Latin trīstis ('sad, sorrowful, mournful, gloomy').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: triste

troca.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Portuguese from trocar ('to exchange, swap, barter').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: troca

trocado.etymology: Past participle of trocar ('to exchange, swap, change money'), used adjectivally ('swapped, inverted') and as a noun ('small change').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trocado

trocar.etymology: Shared with Spanish trocar, Old Occitan trocar, and French troquer ('to barter, exchange'); of uncertain ultimate origin, often linked to a Vulgar Latin *torcāre ('to twist, turn back, invert', from Latin torquēre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: trocar

troco.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Portuguese from trocar ('to exchange, change money'), designating an exchange or the change returned after a purchase.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: troco

trânsito.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin trānsitus ('passage, crossing, going over'), derived from trānsīre ('to go across, pass over', from trāns- 'across' + īre 'to go').

history.meaning: passage, movement of vehicles and pedestrians, traffic

tu.etymology: Inherited from Latin tū ('thou, you', second-person singular nominative pronoun).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tu

tudinho.etymology: Formed in Portuguese as an intensive diminutive of tudo ('all, everything' < Latin tōtum) + the diminutive suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tudinho

tudo.etymology: Inherited from Latin tōtum ('the whole, all, everything', neuter singular of tōtus 'all, whole'), differentiated from masculine todo in Portuguese by raising of the tonic vowel to u.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tudo

táxi.etymology: Borrowed from French taxi, an abbreviation of taximètre ('taximeter cab'), coined from Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, 'arrangement, fixed rate, charge') + μέτρον (métron, 'measure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: táxi

tão.etymology: Inherited from Latin tam ('so, to such a degree'), reinforced in proclitic position by apocope of tanto (< Latin tantum), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese tan to modern tão.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tão

térreo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin terreus ('made of earth, on the ground', derived from terra 'earth, ground'), used in Portuguese both as an adjective and by ellipsis of andar térreo ('ground floor').

history.meaning: of earth, earthen, at ground level

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: térreo

título.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin titulus ('inscription, label, heading, title of honor, legal claim').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: título

uau.etymology: Expressive vocalic interjection of astonishment or admiration, reinforced in modern Portuguese by English wow.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: uau

uf.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection imitating a puff of breath or heavy exhalation of relief, tiredness, or impatience.

history.meaning: exclamation of relief, exhaustion, or annoyance

ufa.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection representing a loud sigh of relief or fatigue (an expanded variant of uf).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ufa

ui.etymology: Expressive natural interjection uttered in response to sudden pain, a scare, or surprise.

history.meaning: ouch!, oops!, oh! (exclamation of pain or surprise)

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ui

um.etymology: Inherited from Latin ūnum (accusative masculine singular of ūnus, 'one, a single'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese ũu to modern um.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: um

usado.etymology: Past participle of usar ('to use, wear'), continuing Vulgar Latin *ūsātus ('used, customary').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: usado

usar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ūsāre ('to use, employ regularly'), a frequentative verb formed on Classical Latin ūsus, past participle of ūtī ('to use, make use of').

history.meaning: to use, wear, be accustomed to

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: usar
