sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: valer

valsa.etymology: Priberam derives valsa from French valse, borrowed from German Walzer ('revolving three-beat dance', from walzen, 'to turn').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: valsa

valsa.notes: Feminine noun in Portuguese (a valsa, Valsa do Pátio), unlike masculine Spanish el vals.

van.etymology: Borrowed from English van ('enclosed motor vehicle for passengers or freight'), itself an aphetic shortening of caravan (< French caravane < Persian kārvān, 'company of travelers').

history.meaning: covered wagon; passenger or cargo van

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: van

varanda.etymology: Attested in Portuguese since the late 15th century (and exported from Portuguese to English veranda via India); of debated ultimate origin, traced either to a pre-Roman Iberian/Celtic word (*anda / *varanda 'railing, balcony') or to Sanskrit varaṇḍa ('portico, gallery').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: varanda

varrer.etymology: Inherited from Latin verrere ('to sweep, brush, drag clean'), with opening of pre-rhotic e to a in Old Galician-Portuguese (verrer > varrer).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: varrer

vaso.etymology: Inherited or adapted from Vulgar Latin vasum (second-declension remodeling of Classical Latin vās, vāsis, 'vessel, dish, pot, container').

history.meaning: vessel, flower pot, vase, toilet bowl

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vaso

vazar.etymology: Derived from vazio ('empty') or inherited from Vulgar Latin *vacuāre ('to make empty, drain, pour out', from Classical Latin vacuus 'empty').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vazar

vazio.etymology: Inherited from Latin vacīvus ('empty, unoccupied, devoid of', a collateral derivative of vacāre 'to be empty' alongside vacuus), with regular voicing of intervocalic -c- before front vowel to -z- and loss of -v-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vazio

veio.etymology: As a noun ('streak in wood or stone, mineral seam, rotating shaft or axle'), formed as a masculine variant of veia ('vein' < Latin vēna, via loss of intervocalic -n-); homonymous with veio ('came'), third-person singular preterite of vir (< Latin vēnit).

history.meaning: wood grain, mineral vein, shaft; came

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: veio

velho.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin veclus, syncopated from Classical Latin vetulus ('old, aged, little old', diminutive of vetus 'old'), with regular Galician-Portuguese palatalization of -cl- to -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: velho

vencer.etymology: Inherited from Latin vincere ('to conquer, overcome, defeat, win').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vencer

venda.etymology: In the commercial sense ('sale, small country shop or inn'), inherited from Late Latin venda, contracted from Classical Latin vēndita (feminine past participle of vēndere 'to sell'); as 'blindfold, bandage', borrowed from Germanic *binda ('band, strip').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: venda

vendedor.etymology: Inherited from Latin vēnditōrem (accusative of vēnditor, 'seller, vendor'), or formed in Portuguese from vender ('to sell') + the agent suffix -dor.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vendedor

vender.etymology: Inherited from Latin vēndere ('to sell, offer for sale', contracted in early Latin from vēnum dare 'to put up for sale').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vender

veneziana.etymology: Priberam records veneziana as the feminine of veneziano, of or from Venice (Veneza). Slatted window shutters became so associated with Venice that the adjective turned into the everyday Brazilian noun for them.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: veneziana

ventilador.etymology: Derived from ventilar ('to fan, air, ventilate' < Latin ventilāre 'to toss in the air, fan, winnow', from ventus 'wind') + the instrumental suffix -dor (compare Latin ventilātor 'winnower').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ventilador

vento.etymology: Inherited from Latin ventus, ventum ('wind, breeze, air in motion').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vento

ver.etymology: Inherited from Latin vidēre ('to see, look at, perceive'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese veer via regular loss of intervocalic -d- and vowel contraction.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ver

verdade.etymology: Inherited from Latin vēritātem (accusative of vēritās, 'truth, reality', derived from vērus 'true'), with syncope of the pretonic vowel -i- and regular voicing of -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: verdade

verdadeiro.etymology: Formed in Old Galician-Portuguese from verdade ('truth' < Latin vēritātem) + the adjectival suffix -eiro (< Latin -ārius).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: verdadeiro

verde.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis ('green, fresh, blooming', from virēre 'to be green').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: verde

vermelho.etymology: Inherited from Latin vermiculus ('little worm; the kermes scale insect used to make crimson dye', diminutive of vermis 'worm'), which came to mean 'scarlet, red' and displaced Classical Latin ruber in Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vermelho

verso.etymology: Borrowed or inherited from Latin versus ('furrow, turning of the plow at the end of a field, line of writing, verse of poetry', from vertere 'to turn').

history.meaning: turning, furrow, line of verse; back side

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: verso

vertical.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin verticālis ('situated at the vertex or overhead zenith, vertical'), derived from Classical Latin vertex, verticis ('whirlpool, crown of the head, peak, zenith', from vertere 'to turn').

history.meaning: overhead, perpendicular to the horizon, vertical

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vertical

verão.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *verānum [tempus] ('springtime season', derived from Classical Latin vēr, 'spring'), with regular loss of intervocalic -n- (*verānu > verão).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: verão

verão.notes: Replaced Classical Latin aestās (preserved only in literary estio) as the everyday word for summer.

vestido.etymology: Inherited from Latin vestītus ('clothed, dressed, adorned'), past participle of vestīre ('to clothe, dress', from vestis 'garment'), used both as an adjective ('dressed') and as a noun ('dress, garment').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vestido

vez.etymology: Inherited from Latin vicem (accusative of defectively attested *vix, genitive vicis, 'change, alternation, turn, succession, occasion').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vez

viagem.etymology: Borrowed via Old Occitan or Catalan viatge from Late Latin viāticum ('journey, trip', originally 'money or provisions for a journey' in Classical Latin, derived from via 'road, way').

history.meaning: road, way -> travel provisions; (Late Latin) journey

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: viagem

vida.etymology: Inherited from Latin vīta ('life, existence, way of life'), with regular Western Iberian voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vida

vidro.etymology: Inherited from Latin vitrum ('glass'), with regular voicing of -tr- to -dr-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vidro

viga.etymology: Shared with Spanish viga ('beam, girder'); usually traced to Latin bīga ('pair of yoked horses, two-wheeled chariot', applied metaphorically to a supporting pair of timbers or crossbeam).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: viga

vigiar.etymology: Inherited from Latin vigilāre ('to be awake, keep watch, guard', derived from vigil 'awake, alert, watchful'; doublet of learned vigilar).

history.meaning: to stay awake, watch over, guard
to watch over, guard, keep an eye on

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vigiar

vinagre.etymology: Borrowed from Old French or Occitan vin aigre ('sour wine'), formed from Latin vīnum ('wine') + ācrem ('sharp, sour').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vinagre

vinagre.notes: Used both in culinary dressings and, diluted in warm water, for streak-free glass cleaning.

vinte.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin vīntī, contracted from Classical Latin vīgintī ('twenty').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vinte

vir.etymology: Inherited from Latin venīre ('to come'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese vĩir via regular loss of intervocalic -n- and vowel contraction.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vir

virado.etymology: Past participle of virar ('to turn, flip, invert'), used adjectivally ('turned, facing, upside down') and nominally.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: virado

virar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vīrāre ('to turn, spin, veer', shared with French virer, Occitan virar, and Spanish virar), generally explained as a blend of Late Latin gyrāre ('to turn in a circle') with vibrāre ('to shake, brandish') or a Celtic root *vīro- ('to twist, deviate').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: virar

visita.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from visitar ('to go to see, visit' < Latin vīsitāre, frequentative of vīsere 'to go to see, look at', from vidēre 'to see').

history.meaning: to see -> to go to see often, visit

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: visita

vista.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vīsta ('sight, view, vision'), feminine of *vīstus, a remodeled past participle of Classical Latin vidēre ('to see').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vista

vivo.etymology: Inherited from Latin vīvus, vīvum ('alive, living, lively', related to vīvere 'to live').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vivo

vizinho.etymology: Inherited from Latin vīcīnus ('neighboring, near; neighbor', derived from vīcus 'hamlet, village, quarter, street'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese vezĩo with palatalization of the nasal hiatus to -nh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vizinho

você.etymology: A contraction of the older address expression vossa mercê. The present word addresses another person while taking third-person verb agreement. Its history as a form of address helps explain why você vai differs from a first-person statement with vou.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: você

vocês.etymology: Plural of você ('you'), which evolved by progressive phonetic wearing down of the deferential title vossa mercê ('Your Grace, Your Mercy', from Latin vestra / vostra + mercēdem) through vossemecê and vosmecê.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vocês

volta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volta ('turn, bend, return'), feminine of *voltus, a regularized past participle of Classical Latin volvere ('to roll, turn round').

history.meaning: to roll, turn -> turn, circuit, return

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: volta

voltar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *voltāre ('to turn, roll back, return', frequentative built on *voltus from Classical Latin volvere 'to roll, turn'), or formed directly from volta + -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: voltar

vontade.etymology: Inherited from Latin voluntātem (accusative of voluntās, 'will, wish, desire, free choice', from velle 'to will, wish'), evolving through Old Galician-Portuguese voontade via loss of intervocalic -l- and vowel contraction.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vontade

vovô.etymology: Formed in Portuguese by affectionate child-speech reduplication of the final stressed syllable of avô ('grandfather' < Vulgar Latin *aviolus, diminutive of Classical Latin avus 'grandfather').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vovô

voz.etymology: Inherited from Latin vōcem (accusative of vōx, 'voice, sound, call, utterance').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: voz

válvula.etymology: Learned borrowing from Modern/Late Latin valvula ('little folding door, pod, anatomical or mechanical valve'), diminutive of Classical Latin valva ('leaf of a double or folding door').

history.meaning: leaf of a folding door -> small flap, valve

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: válvula

xícara.etymology: Priberam gives Spanish jícara as the source of xícara. The Spanish academy dictionary traces jícara to Nahuatl xicalli, a drinking vessel made from a gourd, so the Brazilian coffee cup carries a word from Mexico by way of Spanish.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: xícara
Diccionario de la lengua española (RAE): jícara

zero.etymology: Borrowed from Italian zero (contracted from zefiro, from Medieval Latin zephirum introduced by Fibonacci), which adapted Arabic ṣifr ('empty, nothing, cipher', a semantic calque of Sanskrit śūnya 'void, zero').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: zero

zíper.etymology: Borrowed from American English zipper ('interlocking slide fastener'), originally registered in 1923 as a trademark for rubber boots by the B. F. Goodrich Company, from onomatopoeic zip ('rapid hissing motion') + -er.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: zíper

água.etymology: Inherited from Latin aqua ('water'), with regular Western Iberian voicing of intervocalic -qu- to -gu-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: água

árvore.etymology: Inherited from Latin arbor, arbŏris (accusative arbŏrem, 'tree'), with lenition of post-consonantal -b- > -v-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: árvore

árvore.notes: Kept Classical Latin's feminine gender in Portuguese (a árvore), whereas Spanish el árbol shifted to masculine.

época.etymology: Learned borrowing via Modern Latin epocha from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, 'check, pause, fixed point in time from which an era is reckoned'), derived from ἐπέχειν (epékhein, 'to hold back, stop').

history.meaning: stoppage, astronomical reference point, fixed era

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: época

óculos.etymology: Plural of óculo, a learned borrowing from Latin oculus ('eye'), applied in early modern Europe first to single optical lenses and telescopes and, in the plural, to a pair of spectacles.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: óculos

óleo.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin oleum ('olive oil, oil'), itself an early Mediterranean borrowing akin to Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, 'olive oil, olive tree').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: óleo

ótimo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin optimus ('best, very good, excellent', suppletive superlative of bonus 'good'), with reduction of the cluster -pt- to -t-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ótimo

ônibus.etymology: Borrowed from French omnibus (short for voiture omnibus, 'carriage for all', introduced for public horse-drawn transit in 1820s France), from the Latin dative/ablative plural omnibus ('for all', from omnis 'all, every').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ônibus

último.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ultimus ('farthest, most distant, extreme, last', superlative formed from the stem of uls / ultrā 'beyond').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: último

úmido.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ūmidus (also spelled hūmidus, 'moist, damp, wet, dank', derived from ūmēre 'to be moist, damp').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: úmido

útil.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ūtilis ('useful, serviceable, beneficial, profitable'), derived from ūtī ('to use, make use of').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: útil
